fuentes/rerum-scoticarum-historia/resume.texto: History of Scotland from its legendary origins to 1572, written in humanist Latin. In the first books Buchanan discusses the place names and peoples given by ancient authors and argues that the first inhabitants of Britain and Ireland came from Gaul and from Celtic Hispania, and that British and Gaelic were kindred to the language of the Gauls. The rest is a political history that justifies the deposition of Mary Stuart.

fuentes/rerum-scoticarum-historia/por_qu.texto: It is the first attempt to explain, with linguistic arguments, the kinship of the peoples of the islands with the Gauls, the basis of the later use of “Celtic” for them. Simon James (1999) and John Collis (2003) cite it as the starting point of that tradition. The political part was condemned by the Scottish Parliament in 1584.

fuentes/antiguedad-de-la-nacion-de-los-c.texto: Antiquity of the Nation and Language of the Celts
Book; English translation by David Jones, The Antiquities of Nations (1706)

Pezron combines biblical chronology with Greek myths: the Celts descend from Gomer, son of Japheth; their kings would be the Titans whom the Greeks turned into gods; and their language, the mother of many others, would survive in Breton and Welsh. The etymologies he proposes to prove it are arbitrary.

His English translation of 1706 was widely read in Wales and gave Welsh and Bretons a shared, prestigious past as “Celts.” Both James (1999) and Collis (2003) place it, together with Lhuyd, at the birth of modern Celtic identity. His method was already outdated for the philology of his own time.
English translation of 1706 (The Antiquities of Nations) on Internet Archive

fuentes/archaeologia-britannica/titulo.texto: Archaeologia Britannica, giving some account additional to what has been hitherto publish'd, of the languages, histories and customs of the original inhabitants of Great Britain

fuentes/archaeologia-britannica/soporte.texto: Book (only volume published of a work planned in several)

fuentes/archaeologia-britannica/resumen.texto: Result of Lhuyd’s travels through Wales, Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall and Brittany between 1697 and 1701. It contains a comparative glossary, grammars of Irish, Cornish and Breton, and a catalogue of Welsh and Irish manuscripts. Lhuyd groups these languages together with Gaulish under the name “Celtic,” and distinguishes between those that keep the q sound of Indo-European (Irish, Gaelic) and those that changed it to p (Welsh, Cornish, Breton).

fuentes/archaeologia-britannica/por_que_.texto: It is the founding work of comparative Celtic linguistics, and the one that fixed the term “Celtic” for the languages of the islands, from which the term “Celts” for their speakers came. James (1999) notes that this name was a scholarly classification, not the recovery of an identity that those peoples had.

fuentes/stonehenge-stukeley/titulo.texto: Stonehenge, a Temple Restor'd to the British Druids

fuentes/stonehenge-stukeley/soporte.texto: Book; continued by Abury, a Temple of the British Druids (1743)

fuentes/stonehenge-stukeley/resumen.texto: Description of Stonehenge with plans and views taken between 1719 and 1724, which record details now lost and the orientation of the axis toward the sunrise at the summer solstice. Stukeley attributes the monument to the druids, whom he describes as priests of a patriarchal religion that knew the Trinity and who arrived in Britain after the Flood.

fuentes/stonehenge-stukeley/por_que_impo.texto: It spread the association of Stonehenge with the druids, which neo-druid groups still maintain, although the dating of the monument (around 3000 to 1500 BC) rules it out. Stuart Piggott (1950) used it to show how a good field observer could build a theory with no basis.

fuentes/poemas-de-ossian/soporte.texto: Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760), Fingal (1761, dated 1762), Temora (1763) and The Works of Ossian (1765)

fuentes/poemas-de-ossian/resumen.texto: Epic poems in rhythmic prose that Macpherson presented as translations of Ossian, son of King Fingal, a 3rd-century Gaelic bard, preserved in oral tradition and in manuscripts from the Highlands. They narrate wars of the Caledonians against invaders and against Rome, with a melancholy tone of dead heroes, mists and tombs. The characters come from the Gaelic ballads of the Fionn cycle, which in Ireland and Scotland were Irish and medieval, but Macpherson made them Scottish and ancient.

fuentes/poemas-de-ossian/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the most widely read books in Europe for half a century: Goethe, Herder, Jefferson and Napoleon admired it, and it founded the romantic image of the melancholy, defeated Celt. Hugh Blair defended its authenticity (1763); Samuel Johnson denied it (1775). The Highland Society commission (1805) and Derick Thomson (1952) showed that the poems were free recreations of real ballads.

fuentes/viaje-a-las-islas-occidentales/t.texto: A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland

fuentes/viaje-a-las-islas-occidentales/r.texto: Account of the journey of Johnson and James Boswell through the Highlands and the Hebrides in the autumn of 1773, with observations on clan society, which was being dismantled after 1746, on emigration and on the language. Johnson states that Gaelic had never been a written language, that no Gaelic manuscript more than a hundred years old existed, and that Macpherson could not show the originals of Ossian because they did not exist.

fuentes/viaje-a-las-islas-occidentales/p.texto: It opened the public controversy over Ossian. He was right about the lack of originals and wrong about Gaelic writing, of which medieval manuscripts existed, such as the Book of the Dean of Lismore. It is also a direct testimony of the Highlands before the great clearances.

fuentes/informe-de-la-highland-society-s.texto: Report of the Committee of the Highland Society of Scotland, Appointed to Inquire into the Nature and Authenticity of the Poems of Ossian
Printed report, with appendices of letters and testimonies

After gathering letters from ministers, teachers and elders of the Highlands and reviewing the papers left by Macpherson, the committee concluded that in Gaelic oral tradition there existed poems about Fingal and Ossian with the same character as those published, but that it had found none that matched them in title and content. Its conclusion was that Macpherson had completed, joined and changed a great deal, adding and removing at his pleasure.

It is the most balanced verdict of its time: it treated the work neither as a total forgery nor as a faithful translation. Its conclusion coincides in essence with that of Derick Thomson (1952), who identified the ballads used.

fuentes/boadicea-oda-de-cowper/resumen.texto: Poem in which a druid prophesies to Boudica, scourged by the Romans, that Rome will fall and that her descendants will rule “regions Caesar never knew.” The queen dies invoking the vengeance of heaven.

fuentes/boadicea-oda-de-cowper/por_que_i.texto: It is the text that turned Tacitus’s rebel queen into a forerunner of the British Empire; its verses were engraved on the pedestal of the Westminster statue (1902). It shows how a figure of resistance against one empire became an emblem of another.

fuentes/myvyrian-archaiology/autor.texto: Owen Jones (Myfyr), Iolo Morganwg and William Owen Pughe

fuentes/myvyrian-archaiology/resumen.texto: First great edition of medieval Welsh poetry, chronicles and triads, paid for by Owen Jones, a Welsh furrier in London, with texts copied from manuscripts by Iolo Morganwg and William Owen Pughe. Alongside authentic texts, the third volume includes triads and chronicles that Iolo invented or altered to give Glamorgan and the bards a druidic past.

fuentes/myvyrian-archaiology/por_que_imp.texto: It made much of medieval Welsh literature accessible for the first time, but it mixed the authentic with Iolo’s inventions, which were cited as sources for more than a century. Griffith John Williams separated one from the other in the 1920s.

fuentes/barzaz-breiz/titulo.texto: Barzaz Breiz: Popular Songs of Brittany

fuentes/barzaz-breiz/soporte.texto: Book in two volumes; enlarged editions in 1845 and 1867

fuentes/barzaz-breiz/resumen.texto: Collection of Breton popular songs with French translation, notes and melodies. La Villemarqué arranged them as a history of Brittany in verse, from supposed Druidic songs and sixth-century bards to the Middle Ages and the folklore of his own time.

fuentes/barzaz-breiz/por_que_importa.texto: It was an enormous success and a founding text of the Breton movement. From the 1860s its authenticity was disputed (François-Marie Luzel; Francis Gourvil, 1960). The thesis of Donatien Laurent (1989), based on the field notebooks, showed that many songs were really collected, but that the editor rearranged them and invented an antiquity for them.

fuentes/historia-de-los-galos-thierry/re.texto: History of the Gauls from their first migrations to the Roman conquest, built from all the Greek and Latin authors. Thierry divides the Gauls into two races, the Gauls and the Cymry, explains history through the character of those races, and presents the Gauls as ancestors of most of the French people.

fuentes/historia-de-los-galos-thierry/po.texto: It was the first modern synthesis, and it spread in France the idea of the Gauls as a founding people, which Napoleon III and the Third Republic’s school took up. Its racial explanation did not survive the criticism of later philology and archaeology (Henri Hubert, 1932).

fuentes/eastern-origin-of-the-celtic-nat.texto: The Eastern Origin of the Celtic Nations

Prichard compares the vocabulary, pronouns, numerals and conjugation of Welsh, Irish and the other Celtic languages with Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and the Germanic languages, and concludes that they belong to the same family, Indo-European.
It is one of the first demonstrations that the Celtic languages are Indo-European, together with Bopp and Pictet. Zeuss (1853) made it indisputable with a more rigorous method.

fuentes/afinidad-de-las-lenguas-celticas.texto: On the Affinity of the Celtic Languages with Sanskrit
Comparative study of the sounds, vocabulary and grammar of Irish, Gaelic, Welsh, Cornish and Breton against Sanskrit, showing regular correspondences among them.
With Bopp’s work (1838) it closed the discussion over whether the Celtic languages were Indo-European, and with it the discussion of the Celtomaniacs, who made them the mother of all languages.

fuentes/mabinogion-de-guest/resumen.texto: English translation, with the Welsh text and notes, of the eleven prose tales of the Red Book of Hergest and the White Book of Rhydderch (the four branches of the Mabinogi, the Arthurian tales and others), plus the story of Taliesin, which comes from later manuscripts. Guest took the name Mabinogion from a form that appears only once in the manuscripts.

fuentes/mabinogion-de-guest/por_que_impo.texto: She made medieval Welsh prose known across Europe and influenced Victorian Arthurian literature. Her Taliesin comes from late copies, some of which passed through the hands of Iolo Morganwg; later translations replaced it on philological grounds.

fuentes/grammatica-celtica/resumen.texto: Historical grammar of the Celtic languages, written in Latin from the Old Irish and Old Welsh glosses in the Würzburg, Milan, St. Gall, Karlsruhe and other manuscripts, and from the known Gaulish inscriptions. It establishes the correspondences between the Celtic languages and the other Indo-European ones, and clearly separates the Gaelic and British branches.

fuentes/grammatica-celtica/por_que_impor.texto: It founded Celtic philology as a scientific discipline and ended the fantastic etymologies of the Celtomaniacs. Its comparative method is the basis of all later study of the Celtic languages.

fuentes/la-poesia-de-las-razas-celticas/.texto: The Poetry of the Celtic Races
Essay published in the Revue des Deux Mondes

Renan’s essay, written by a Breton, on Welsh and Breton literature, based on Guest’s translation of the Mabinogion and on La Villemarqué’s collection. It describes the “Celtic races” as timid, idealistic, melancholic and feminine, inclined to loyalty to lost causes and defeated by the more practical races.

It fixed the romantic stereotype of the dreaming, defeated Celt, which Matthew Arnold took up in 1867 and which reached popular culture. Malcolm Chapman (1992) analyzes it as an image constructed from the center, which attributes to the periphery what the center says it does not have.

fuentes/historia-de-julio-cesar-napoleon.texto: Book in two volumes, with an atlas; left unfinished

Biography of Caesar written by the emperor with the help of a team of scholars and soldiers, based on the excavations he had carried out at Alesia, Gergovia and other sites. The preface holds that great men are sent by Providence to fulfill a mission, an argument read as a justification of the two Napoleons.

It promoted the military archaeology of the conquest of Gaul and fixed the location of Alesia at Alise-Sainte-Reine, confirmed in the 1990s. At the same time it used ancient history to legitimize the Second Empire, as Michael Dietler (1994) points out.

fuentes/on-the-study-of-celtic-literatur.texto: On the Study of Celtic Literature
Book based on lectures given at Oxford (1865-1866)

Arnold praises Welsh and Irish literature and calls for it to be studied at the universities, but he attributes to the “Celtic genius” feeling, rebellion against “the despotism of fact” and a lack of political sense. He proposes that English replace the Celtic languages as the practical language while their literature is preserved.

It influenced the creation of the Celtic chair at Oxford (1877) and the Victorian image of the Celt. It was criticized for fixing racial stereotypes and for subordinating Celtic cultures to English (Rachel Bromwich, 1965; Malcolm Chapman, 1992).

fuentes/leyes-de-gales-1535-1542/soporte.texto: Acts of Parliament (27 Hen. VIII c. 26 and 34 & 35 Hen. VIII c. 26)

fuentes/leyes-de-gales-1535-1542/resumen.texto: Acts of Henry VIII that incorporated Wales into the kingdom of England, divided its territory into counties, applied English law there and gave it members in Parliament. The so-called language clause provided that the courts would work in English and that no one who used Welsh could hold public office unless he also used English.

fuentes/leyes-de-gales-1535-1542/por_que.texto: It left Welsh out of administration and justice and separated the Welsh nobility from it, although the language remained the language of the people for three more centuries. What remained of the language clause was repealed in 1993.

fuentes/biblia-galesa-de-1588/soporte.texto: Printed book; revised by Richard Parry and John Davies in 1620

fuentes/biblia-galesa-de-1588/resumen.texto: First complete translation of the Bible into Welsh, made by William Morgan from Hebrew and Greek by order of a 1563 law that required the Bible and the prayer book to be translated into Welsh for the churches of Wales. It uses a literary language based on the tradition of the medieval poets.

fuentes/biblia-galesa-de-1588/por_que_im.texto: It gave Welsh a written standard and a place in weekly worship, which Sunday schools and Methodism later extended. Historians of Welsh count it among the causes of the language’s survival, unlike Cornish, which had no printed Bible.

fuentes/estatutos-de-iona/soporte.texto: Agreement imposed on the chiefs of the Hebridean clans, ratified by the Privy Council

fuentes/estatutos-de-iona/resumen.texto: Agreement that Bishop Andrew Knox had the chiefs of the Hebridean clans sign in the name of James VI. It obliged them to maintain Protestant churches, limit their armed retinues and wine consumption, expel bards and vagrants, and send their heirs to study in English-speaking schools in the Lowlands.

fuentes/estatutos-de-iona/por_que_import.texto: It was the first step in a written policy to separate the elites of the Highlands from the Gaelic language and culture, which a Privy Council act of 1616 completed by ordering that English be planted everywhere and that Gaelic, which it called a cause of barbarity, be abolished.

fuentes/descubrimiento-de-las-verdaderas.texto: A Discovery of the True Causes why Ireland was never Entirely Subdued

Treatise by the Attorney General of Ireland, the Englishman John Davies, which explains the failure of four centuries of conquest by the fact that the English settlers had adopted Irish laws and customs. He describes and condemns the law of the brehons (the traditional judges), succession by tanistry and the division of lands among kinsmen, which the English courts had just declared void.
It is the main source on the end of traditional Irish law, written by one of the jurists who abolished it. It describes in detail what it combats and judges it from English law.

fuentes/expiracion-de-la-lengua-cornica-.texto: On the Expiration of the Cornish Language
Letter to John Lloyd, read at the Society of Antiquaries of London in 1773 and published in its journal Archaeologia, vol. III (1775)

Barrington recounts his search for Cornish speakers in Cornwall in 1768 and his visit to Mousehole, where Dolly Pentreath, an elderly fishwife, spoke to him fluently in Cornish. He adds that two neighbors somewhat younger understood it, although they did not speak it with ease.

It is the testimony that turned Dolly Pentreath into the “last speaker” of Cornish. Barrington himself later published the letter in Cornish from the fisherman William Bodinar (1776), which said that he knew five other people who spoke it in Mousehole, so his conclusion was already then an oversimplification.
Archaeologia, vol. III (1775), on Internet Archive

fuentes/informe-barere-1794/titulo.texto: Report of the Committee of Public Safety on Languages

fuentes/informe-barere-1794/soporte.texto: Report read to the National Convention on 8 Pluviôse, Year II (27 January 1794)

fuentes/informe-barere-1794/resumen.texto: Barère argues that regional languages serve the enemies of the Revolution: “federalism and superstition speak in Breton, emigration and hatred of the Republic speak German, counter-revolution speaks Italian and fanaticism speaks Basque.” He proposes sending French teachers to all the municipalities where those languages were spoken.

fuentes/informe-barere-1794/por_que_impo.texto: Together with the Abbé Grégoire’s report of the same year on the need to destroy the patois, it fixed the doctrine of a nation with a single language, which the Third Republic’s school applied to Breton.

fuentes/informe-sobre-la-educacion-en-ga.texto: Reports of the Commissioners of Inquiry into the State of Education in Wales
Ralph Lingen, Jelinger Symons and Henry Vaughan Johnson
Official report in three volumes, with blue covers

Survey commissioned by Parliament on the schools of Wales, carried out by three English Anglican commissioners who did not speak Welsh and who relied on testimony from clergy of their own denomination. Besides the poverty of the schools, they attributed the ignorance, dirtiness and immorality of the people, and especially of the women, to the Welsh language and to Nonconformist Protestantism.

In Wales it was called “the treachery of the Blue Books” (Brad y Llyfrau Gleision) and provoked a national reaction. At the same time it reinforced the idea that progress came through English. In some schools, without it being official policy, the Welsh Not was used: a board hung around the neck of a pupil who spoke Welsh.
Reports of the Commissioners (1847-1848) on Internet Archive

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-1851/titulo.texto: The Census of Ireland for the Year 1851

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-1851/resumen.texto: First Irish census to ask about language. It counted 6.55 million inhabitants, compared with 8.18 million in 1841, and some 1.5 million people who spoke Irish (23% of the population), of whom about 320,000 spoke only Irish, concentrated in the west.

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-1851/por_que.texto: It measures the effect of the Great Famine on the population and on the language. Historians (Garret FitzGerald, among others) believe it underestimated the number of Irish speakers, because Irish was seen as a sign of poverty and many did not declare it.

fuentes/the-necessity-for-de-anglicising.texto: Lecture to the Irish National Literary Society (25 November 1892), published in 1894

Hyde argues that the Irish imitate England in everything while saying they hate her, and that the nation can exist only if it recovers what distinguishes it: the Irish language, names, music, games and customs. He proposes saving Irish where it is still spoken and teaching it in the schools, and presents his program as one above parties and religions.

It is the founding text of the Gaelic revival: a year later Hyde founded the Gaelic League. The idea of a nation defined by language and culture influenced the generation that achieved independence, although Hyde wanted to keep the League out of politics.
In The Revival of Irish Literature (1894), on Internet Archive

fuentes/the-celtic-twilight/resumen.texto: Collection of short tales about fairies, apparitions and beliefs that Yeats heard from peasants in Sligo and Galway, told in a poetic and personal tone.

fuentes/the-celtic-twilight/por_que_impo.texto: Its title gave a name to an aesthetic of the Irish literary revival, made of mystery, melancholy and an invisible world, which later critics associated with the image of the dreamy Celt of Renan and Arnold.

fuentes/hanes-y-wladfa-gymreig/resumen.texto: History of the Welsh colony of Chubut from the preparation of the voyage of the Mimosa to the early 1890s, written by one of the ministers who arrived in 1865. It tells of the landing, the hunger of the first years, the help of the Tehuelches, the irrigation canals and relations with the Argentine government.

fuentes/hanes-y-wladfa-gymreig/por_que_i.texto: It is the first history written by a protagonist, in Welsh and for Welsh readers. Its account of a peaceful colony with good relations with the Tehuelches became the basis of the community’s memory, and it is discussed today in light of the Conquest of the Desert and the dispossession of Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/carmina-gadelica/soporte.texto: Two volumes in 1900; four more, edited by his descendants and others, between 1940 and 1971

fuentes/carmina-gadelica/resumen.texto: Collection of prayers, hymns, blessings, charms and work formulas gathered by Carmichael between 1860 and 1909 in the Hebrides and the Highlands, with English translation. It mixes Christian invocations, mainly Catholic ones, with formulas of protection for livestock, fire and travel.

fuentes/carmina-gadelica/por_que_importa.texto: It became the main source of modern “Celtic spirituality.” Hamish Robertson (1976) and John Lorne Campbell (1978) showed, by comparison with the field notebooks, that Carmichael polished, completed and archaized many texts, so that it is not a faithful transcription of oral tradition.

fuentes/cuchulain-of-muirthemne/soporte.texto: Book, with preface by W. B. Yeats

fuentes/cuchulain-of-muirthemne/resumen.texto: English version of the sagas of the Ulster cycle, centered on Cú Chulainn and the Cattle Raid of Cooley, assembled by Lady Gregory from scholarly translations and written in the English of western Ireland, which keeps the syntax of Irish. It softens or omits the violent and sexual passages of the originals.

fuentes/cuchulain-of-muirthemne/por_que_.texto: It brought the Irish sagas to a broad public and gave the writers of the literary revival their heroic themes. It is an example of how the medieval tradition was adapted to the taste and morality of the nationalism of its time.

fuentes/handbook-of-the-cornish-language.texto: A Handbook of the Cornish Language, chiefly in its latest stages

Practical grammar of Cornish based on the language of the last texts of the 17th and 18th centuries, with a new spelling, designed so that the people of Cornwall could learn it again. Asked why they should learn it if it brought them no benefit, Jenner answers in the introduction: “because they are from Cornwall.”

It began the revival of Cornish. Robert Morton Nance later preferred to base the language on the medieval texts (Unified Cornish, 1929), and the debate between varieties lasted until the Standard Written Form of 2008.

fuentes/tynged-yr-iaith/resumen.texto: The writer and founder of the Welsh nationalist party announced that, if the trend of the censuses continued, Welsh would cease to be spoken as a living language at the beginning of the 21st century, and he argued that saving it mattered more than political autonomy. He called for revolutionary methods, such as refusing to pay taxes or to fill in forms that were not in Welsh.

fuentes/tynged-yr-iaith/por_que_importa.texto: It led to the founding of the Welsh Language Society (Cymdeithas yr Iaith Gymraeg) in 1962 and to its civil disobedience campaign, which brought about the Welsh language acts of 1967 and 1993 and Welsh-language television.

fuentes/ley-de-la-lengua-galesa-1993/res.texto: Act that established that Welsh and English must be treated on an equal basis in public administration and justice, created the Welsh Language Board and obliged public bodies to have Welsh language schemes. It repealed what remained of the 1536 language clause.

fuentes/ley-de-la-lengua-galesa-1993/por.texto: It was the broadest legal recognition that a Celtic language had in the United Kingdom, and the basis for the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011, which gave it official status in Wales.

fuentes/ley-del-gaelico-2005/soporte.texto: Act of the Scottish Parliament (2005 asp 7)

fuentes/ley-del-gaelico-2005/resumen.texto: First law to recognize Gaelic as an official language of Scotland, “with equal respect” to English. It created the body Bòrd na Gàidhlig and required a national Gaelic plan and plans in public bodies.

fuentes/ley-del-gaelico-2005/por_que_imp.texto: It came when the 2001 census counted fewer than 60,000 speakers. Later censuses show an increase in the number of people with some knowledge, above all through schooling in Gaelic.

fuentes/constitucion-de-irlanda-1937/sop.texto: Constitution approved by referendum on 1 July 1937

fuentes/constitucion-de-irlanda-1937/res.texto: Its Article 8 declares that Irish, as the national language, is the first official language and recognizes English as the second official language. In case of difference between the two versions, the Irish text prevails.

fuentes/constitucion-de-irlanda-1937/por.texto: It enshrined the language policy of the Irish State since 1922, which made the teaching of Irish compulsory in schools and protected the Irish-speaking areas (the Gaeltacht), without achieving its return as the everyday language of the majority.

fuentes/constitucion-de-irlanda-1937/lee.texto: Official text in force, on the Irish Statute Book

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-2022/titulo.texto: Census 2022 Profile 8 – The Irish Language and Education

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-2022/resumen.texto: Of 1,873,997 people over the age of three who said they could speak Irish (40% of those who answered the question), almost 473,000 said they never spoke it, and 553,965 said they spoke it only within the education system. Those who used it every day outside the education system numbered 71,968: 20,261 in the Gaeltacht and 51,707 outside it.

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-2022/por_que.texto: It shows the gap between the widespread school knowledge of Irish and its daily use, which is limited to a minority.

fuentes/censo-de-irlanda-de-2022/leer.0..texto: Official report of the Central Statistics Office

fuentes/censo-de-escocia-de-2022/resumen.texto: 2.5% of Scotland’s population over the age of three, 130,161 people, declared some knowledge of Gaelic (speaking, reading, writing or understanding it), 43,100 more than in 2011. 69,701 said they could speak it, compared with 57,375 in 2011. In the Outer Hebrides (Na h-Eileanan Siar) 57.2% had some knowledge, and in the rest of the country, except Highland and Argyll and Bute, less than 3%.

fuentes/censo-de-escocia-de-2022/por_que.texto: It is the first increase in more than a century. It is attributed to schooling in Gaelic and to adults who learn it; speakers in the traditional Hebridean communities continue to decline.

fuentes/censo-de-escocia-de-2022/leer.0..texto: Official report of National Records of Scotland (21 May 2024), with the section on Gaelic

fuentes/censo-de-gales-de-2021/resumen.texto: 538,300 residents of Wales over the age of three, 17.8% of the population, declared that they could speak Welsh, some 24,000 fewer than in 2011 (19.0%). The question measures the declared ability to speak the language, not how often it is used.

fuentes/censo-de-gales-de-2021/por_que_i.texto: The government of Wales’s annual surveys give higher figures, because they ask in a different way; the difference shows how hard it is to measure bilingualism. The Welsh government has set itself the goal of reaching a million speakers by 2050.

fuentes/censo-de-gales-de-2021/leer.0.ti.texto: Official bulletin of the Office for National Statistics

fuentes/encuesta-sobre-el-breton-2024/ti.texto: Sociolinguistic survey on the languages of Brittany (2024)

fuentes/encuesta-sobre-el-breton-2024/au.texto: Brittany Region and the TMO Régions institute

fuentes/encuesta-sobre-el-breton-2024/so.texto: Telephone survey of 8,336 inhabitants of the five departments of historic Brittany (30 August to 8 November 2024), published on 20 January 2025

fuentes/encuesta-sobre-el-breton-2024/re.texto: 2.7% of respondents said they spoke Breton very well or fairly well, which the institute translates into about 107,000 people (between 93,000 and 120,000), compared with 214,000 in the 2018 survey by the same institute. The average age of Breton speakers dropped from 70 to about 58, transmission within families has fallen and the number of learners is growing. Gallo, the Romance language of Upper Brittany, would have some 132,000 speakers.

fuentes/encuesta-sobre-el-breton-2024/po.texto: It measures the collapse of Breton from more than a million speakers around 1950, according to estimates by Fañch Broudic, despite bilingual schooling and the Diwan schools. Some critics pointed out that only 307 respondents said they spoke Breton, and they disputed the weighting used to extrapolate the figure.

fuentes/historia-de-galicia-murguia/resu.texto: History of Galicia from the first settlers to the Middle Ages. Murguía argues that the Galicians descend from Celts who arrived in remote times, that this root was preserved in their character, customs and monuments (he attributed the castros and the megaliths to the Celts), and that it distinguishes Galicia from the rest of Spain.

fuentes/historia-de-galicia-murguia/por_.texto: It gave Galician regionalism (galleguismo) its myth of origin, which Eduardo Pondal brought into poetry and which reached the Galician anthem. Beatriz Díaz Santana (2002) and others showed that it rested on etymologies and analogies without basis and on a racial idea of the nation. Current archaeology debates whether the castro culture can be called Celtic.

fuentes/queixumes-dos-pinos/resumen.texto: Book of poems in Galician, published in Buenos Aires, in which Pondal sings of an oppressed Galicia of Celtic bards and warriors and calls for its awakening. Its heroic and archaizing tone is inspired by Macpherson’s Ossian.

fuentes/queixumes-dos-pinos/por_que_impo.texto: It is the literary peak of nineteenth-century Galician Celticism. Its author wrote shortly afterwards “Os pinos,” the lyrics of the Galician anthem.

fuentes/historia-de-la-galia-jullian/res.texto: History of Gaul from the first settlers to the end of the Roman Empire, with all the written sources and the archaeology available. Jullian sees in independent Gaul a nation in formation, in Vercingetorix its hero, and in the Roman conquest a rupture that halted a development of its own, though he acknowledges the achievements of Roman Gaul.

fuentes/historia-de-la-galia-jullian/por.texto: It was the great French synthesis for half a century and fixed in schools the image of the Gauls as ancestors of the nation. Christian Goudineau (1990, 2001) and later archaeology revised his patriotic reading and his trust in Caesar’s account.

fuentes/les-celtes-hubert/soporte.texto: Two volumes, published after the author’s death by Marcel Mauss and other disciples

fuentes/les-celtes-hubert/resumen.texto: Synthesis on the origin, expansion and civilization of the Celts, combining linguistics, archaeology, classical sources and Irish and Welsh texts. Hubert explains the Celtic expansion in waves from central Europe and describes their society and religion using Durkheim’s sociological method.

fuentes/les-celtes-hubert/por_que_import.texto: It was the great French synthesis of the interwar period and the basis of the model of an expansion from central Europe, which Collis (2003) and the supporters of an Atlantic origin later debated. His rejection of racial explanations separates him from his predecessors.

fuentes/the-celts-powell/soporte.texto: Book in the series Ancient Peoples and Places

fuentes/the-celts-powell/resumen.texto: Popular synthesis of the archaeology, history and religion of the Celts, from Hallstatt to early Ireland, which uses medieval Irish texts to illustrate the society of the continental Iron Age.

fuentes/the-celts-powell/por_que_importa.texto: It was the book through which a generation of readers in English was educated, and one of those that most fixed the idea of a common Celtic culture from Ireland to Anatolia. The Celtic sceptics (James, 1999; Collis, 2003) cite it as an example of that model.

fuentes/the-oldest-irish-tradition/titul.texto: The Oldest Irish Tradition: A Window on the Iron Age

fuentes/the-oldest-irish-tradition/sopor.texto: Rede Lecture of the University of Cambridge, published as a book

fuentes/the-oldest-irish-tradition/resum.texto: Jackson compares the customs of the Ulster cycle (chariot combat, severed heads, the hero’s portion, feasts) with what Posidonius, Diodorus and Strabo say about the Gauls, and concludes that the sagas preserve, through oral tradition, a picture of pre-Christian Iron Age society.

fuentes/the-oldest-irish-tradition/por_q.texto: It was the classic expression of the “nativist” reading. J. P. Mallory showed in the 1980s that most of the objects in the Táin (weapons, brooches, buildings) date from the 7th to the 10th centuries, and Kim McCone (1990) that the sagas are literary works by medieval clerics.

fuentes/william-stukeley-piggott/resumen.texto: Biography of Stukeley that distinguishes the good field observer of his early years from the clergyman who later built a druidic theology on Stonehenge and Avebury, and places his ideas within the search for a natural religion of his time.

fuentes/william-stukeley-piggott/por_que.texto: It is the first critical study of the origin of the modern image of the druids, which Piggott expanded in The Druids (1968).

fuentes/the-celts-construction-of-a-myth.texto: The Celts: The Construction of a Myth

Anthropological study arguing that “Celt” was always a category applied from outside: first by Greeks and Romans to the barbarians of the north, and later by antiquarians and Romantics to the peripheries of France and Great Britain. Chapman analyzes how the center attributed to those peripheries the traits it denied in itself: emotion, irrationality, mystery.

It opened the debate of the 1990s on the invention of the Celtic. It was objected that it reduces to an outside construction a linguistic and literary reality that can be verified (Patrick Sims-Williams, 1998).

fuentes/our-ancestors-the-gauls-dietler/.texto: «Our Ancestors the Gauls»: Archaeology, Ethnic Nationalism, and the Manipulation of Celtic Identity in Modern Europe

Dietler studies the political uses of the Celts in France (Napoleon III and Alesia, the Third Republic, Vichy, Mitterrand and Bibracte), in regional nationalisms and in the European project of the 1990s, and shows how archaeology gave scientific authority to those identities.
It is the main reference on the political uses of the Gauls in modern France. His critique of the 1991 Venice exhibition and of “Celtic Europe” was taken up by British Celtic sceptics.

fuentes/ancient-celts-and-modern-ethnici.texto: J. V. S. Megaw and M. Ruth Megaw

The Megaws, specialists in Celtic art, respond to critics of the idea of the Celts. They argue that La Tène art and the languages show a common reality, and that denying the Celts of the islands is a stance with political undertones: that of an English nationalism which, faced with the devolution of powers to Scotland and Wales, prefers to strip them of their history.

It made the political component of the debate explicit. Simon James (1998) and John Collis (1997) replied in the same journal that their criticism was scientific and that the accusation reversed the terms, because Celticism also had political uses.

fuentes/celtomania-and-celtoscepticism/s.texto: Article in Cambrian Medieval Celtic Studies 36, pp. 1-35

fuentes/celtomania-and-celtoscepticism/r.texto: Critical review of the two extremes: Celtomania, which projects a homogeneous and continuous Celtic culture from antiquity to today, and Celtoscepticism, which denies that the term has any content. Sims-Williams defends a strictly linguistic use of “Celtic” and shows the errors of both positions.

fuentes/celtomania-and-celtoscepticism/p.texto: It is the most cited intervention from linguistics, midway between critics and defenders. His proposal to call Celtic whatever relates to the Celtic languages was accepted by many on both sides. Raimund Karl (2004) considered it insufficient, because it leaves out archaeology and texts.

fuentes/the-atlantic-celts/titulo.texto: The Atlantic Celts: Ancient People or Modern Invention?

fuentes/the-atlantic-celts/resumen.texto: James argues that the Iron Age of Britain and Ireland shows great regional variety and not a common Celtic culture brought by invaders, that no ancient text calls the inhabitants of the islands Celts, and that their Celtic identity was constructed from 1700 onward by Lhuyd, Pezron and Romanticism. He does not deny the kinship of the languages or the reality of the cultures he studies.

fuentes/the-atlantic-celts/por_que_impor.texto: It was the book that brought Celtoscepticism to the general public, and it provoked the reaction of the Megaws and of John Koch. Later archaeology broadly accepted its critique of the invasion model. Ancient DNA (Patterson et al., 2022) later showed a migration from France in the Middle and Late Bronze Age, which its authors propose as the route by which the first Celtic languages reached Britain.

fuentes/celtic-christianity-bradley/titu.texto: Celtic Christianity: Making Myths and Chasing Dreams

fuentes/celtic-christianity-bradley/resu.texto: Bradley, a minister of the Church of Scotland who had earlier written books on Celtic spirituality, surveys the successive waves of enthusiasm for a “Celtic Christianity” from the Middle Ages (Bede, the lives of saints) to the movement of the 1990s, and shows how each era attributed its own ideals to it.

fuentes/celtic-christianity-bradley/por_.texto: Its value lies in the author’s review of his own participation in the movement. He agrees with Donald Meek (2000) and with Wendy Davies that there was no separate “Celtic Church” apart from Rome.

fuentes/the-quest-for-celtic-christianit.texto: Meek, a native Gaelic speaker from the island of Tiree and professor of Celtic studies, argues that the “Celtic Christianity” of modern religious literature (ecological, egalitarian, favorable to women, close to nature and opposed to Rome) is a construction of the late twentieth century, which uses sources such as the Carmina Gadelica without criticism and ignores the medieval sources.
It is the most detailed critique of the movement from within the Gaelic tradition. Its defenders reply that the movement is a present-day spirituality and not a historical thesis.

fuentes/les-celtes-kruta/resumen.texto: Historical synthesis of the continental and insular Celts, followed by a dictionary of more than a thousand entries on peoples, places, gods, objects and authors. Kruta presents the Celts as a civilization with unity of language, art and religion, spread over much of Europe.

fuentes/les-celtes-kruta/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most complete reference work in French. It is also an example of the model criticized by James and Collis: that of a pan-European Celtic civilization, which the 1991 Venice exhibition presented as “the first Europe.”

fuentes/le-dossier-vercingetorix/resumen.texto: Goudineau gathers and comments on all the ancient texts about Vercingetorix (Caesar, Plutarch, Florus, Cassius Dio and the coins) and shows how little is known of him with certainty. In the second part he follows the construction of the hero since the 19th century: Thierry, Henri Martin, Napoleon III, the school of the Third Republic and Vichy.

fuentes/le-dossier-vercingetorix/por_que.texto: It is the reference for separating the historical figure from the myth. Goudineau argues that almost everything known passes through Caesar, who magnified Vercingetorix in order to magnify his own victory.

fuentes/the-celts-origins-myths-inventio.texto: The Celts: Origins, Myths and Inventions

Collis traces the use of the name “Celt” from Hecataeus and Herodotus, who applied it to peoples of Gaul and Iberia, to its extension to Britain and Ireland in the 18th century and to the archaeology of Hallstatt and La Tène in the 19th. He argues that the model of a Celtic homeland in central Europe, from which people, language and culture spread, is a construction of 19th-century archaeology without support in the data.

Together with James’s book, it is the central text of Celtoscepticism, and its review of the ancient sources is much cited. Raimund Karl and John Koch objected that it disregarded linguistic evidence. The thesis of “Celts from the west” (Koch and Cunliffe) took up its critique of the central European model, though to propose another origin.

fuentes/celtoescepticismo-karl/titulo.texto: Celtoscepticism, a convenient excuse for ignoring non-archaeological evidence?

fuentes/celtoescepticismo-karl/soporte.texto: Chapter in E. Sauer (ed.), Archaeology and Ancient History: Breaking Down the Boundaries (London, Routledge)

fuentes/celtoescepticismo-karl/resumen.texto: Karl argues that Celtoscepticists define the Celts only through archaeology and, finding no common material culture, conclude that they did not exist, without attending to language, ancient texts or medieval literature. He proposes defining the Celtic by a combination of linguistic, cultural and documentary traits.

fuentes/celtoescepticismo-karl/por_que_i.texto: It is the most systematic response to Celtoscepticism from archaeology. Its critics reproach its broad definition for once again gathering under one name very different phenomena.

fuentes/celtic-culture-koch/soporte.texto: Encyclopedia in five volumes, with more than a hundred authors

fuentes/celtic-culture-koch/resumen.texto: Encyclopedia on the Celtic-speaking peoples from the Bronze Age to today: languages, archaeology, history, literature, religion, music and diasporas, including the Welsh colony in Patagonia. Koch defines the Celtic by language and brings together authors of different positions.

fuentes/celtic-culture-koch/por_que_impo.texto: It is the broadest reference work in the field and a practical response to Celtoscepticism: it shows the unity of the field of study without asserting a common ethnic identity.

fuentes/blood-of-the-isles/titulo.texto: Blood of the Isles: Exploring the Genetic Roots of Our Tribal History

fuentes/blood-of-the-isles/soporte.texto: Book; in the United States, Saxons, Vikings, and Celts (2006)

fuentes/blood-of-the-isles/resumen.texto: Sykes analyzes the mitochondrial and Y-chromosome DNA of thousands of living people from Britain and Ireland and concludes that most descend from settlers who arrived before the Iron Age, that the Anglo-Saxon and Viking contributions were smaller, and that the lineages he calls “Celtic” are related to the Iberian Peninsula.

fuentes/blood-of-the-isles/por_que_impor.texto: It popularized the idea of a “Celtic” genetic continuity in the islands. It drew criticism for inferring ancient history only from the DNA of living people and for its links to the sale of ancestry tests; later ancient DNA disproved continuity since the Neolithic.

fuentes/the-origins-of-the-british/titul.texto: The Origins of the British: A Genetic Detective Story

fuentes/the-origins-of-the-british/resum.texto: Oppenheimer argues that about three quarters of the islands' ancestry comes from settlers who arrived after the last glaciation from a refuge in southern Europe, that Celtic languages may have reached the islands along the Atlantic coast in the Neolithic, and that the Germanic presence in England predates the Anglo-Saxons.

fuentes/the-origins-of-the-british/por_q.texto: It had wide circulation and was criticized by linguists (his hypothesis about English has no support) and by geneticists, because dating migrations with the DNA of living people is unreliable. Ancient DNA (Olalde et al., 2018) showed a replacement of around 90 % of Britain's population with the arrival of the Bell Beaker culture.

fuentes/identity-and-power-fernandez-got.texto: Identity and Power: The Transformation of Iron Age Societies in Northeast Gaul
Book (Amsterdam University Press, Amsterdam Archaeological Studies series 21)

A study of the Treveri and their neighbors from the early Iron Age to the Roman conquest, which analyzes sanctuaries, oppida, and assembly places as centers of collective identities. Fernández-Götz proposes that these societies had ethnic identities at several levels (the family, the local community, the civitas, and larger groups) that changed over time.
It offers a way out of the debate with the Celtic skeptics: it does not assume a homogeneous Celtic people, but it does not give up on studying collective identities in the Iron Age either.

fuentes/estructura-genetica-britanica-le.texto: The fine-scale genetic structure of the British population
Stephen Leslie, Bruce Winney, Garrett Hellenthal, Peter Donnelly, Walter Bodmer et al.

The study analyzed the genomes of 2,039 people from the United Kingdom whose four grandparents had been born in the same rural area, and found very local genetic groups that partly match former kingdoms. The populations of Wales, Scotland, Cornwall, and Northern Ireland do not form a common “Celtic” group: on the contrary, they are among the most different from one another. It estimated that the Anglo-Saxons contributed less than half of the ancestry of central and southern England.
It is the most cited refutation of the idea of a shared Celtic genetics. Its authors warn that the differences are small and reflect mainly local isolation and migrations after the Roman Empire.

fuentes/diccionario-de-la-lengua-espanol.texto: Real Academia Española and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española

The normative dictionary of Spanish, which gives the etymology of each word. It records as of Celtic or Gaulish origin, among others, camino, camisa, carro, cerveza, legua, berro, brío, colmena (with doubt), sayo, alondra, vasallo, embajada, cambiar, pieza, tonel, landa, losa, tranca, serna, and bresca; it attributes lanza to the Celtiberians, and galgo comes from Latin gallicus, “of Gaul”.
It makes it possible to check which Castilian words have a Celtic origin according to the academic standard, and which do not: álamo comes from Gothic, and gancho and garza are of uncertain origin.
Online consultation (example: the entry “camino”, with its Celtic etymology)

fuentes/dcech-corominas/titulo.texto: Critical Etymological Dictionary of Castilian and Hispanic

fuentes/dcech-corominas/autor.texto: Joan Corominas and José Antonio Pascual

fuentes/dcech-corominas/resumen.texto: The reference etymological dictionary of Spanish, which discusses for each word the hypotheses of origin and the earliest documentation. For many words Corominas proposed a Celtic or pre-Roman origin, sometimes with arguments that have been debated.

fuentes/dcech-corominas/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source of much of the Celtic etymologies of Castilian that the academic dictionary records; its boldest proposals of Celtic origin were later reviewed case by case.

fuentes/dictionnaire-de-la-langue-gauloi.texto: Book, second revised edition (the first is from 2001)
A dictionary of the Gaulish words known from inscriptions, ancient authors, personal and place names, and loanwords into Latin and the Romance languages, with their Indo-European etymology.
It is the most widely used reference for the etymologies of place names such as Lugdunum or Mediolanum; some of its interpretations of proper names are hypotheses that other linguists do not accept.

fuentes/la-langue-gauloise-lambert/resum.texto: A manual of the Gaulish language: its writing, its grammar, its vocabulary, the main inscriptions (Chamalières, Larzac, Coligny, La Graufesenque), and the evidence for its disappearance. It devotes a chapter to Gaulish words that passed into French.

fuentes/la-langue-gauloise-lambert/por_q.texto: It is the standard introduction to Gaulish and the basis of almost all the lists of words of Gaulish origin in French.

fuentes/the-desert-and-the-dream/titulo.texto: The Desert and the Dream: A Study of Welsh Colonization in Chubut 1865-1915

fuentes/the-desert-and-the-dream/resumen.texto: A social history of the Welsh colony in Chubut from Michael D. Jones's idea until 1915: the recruitment of settlers, irrigated agriculture, the Chubut Mercantile Company, the conflicts with the Argentine state over military service and schooling, and the arrival of immigrants of other origins.

fuentes/the-desert-and-the-dream/por_que.texto: It is the basic academic study of Y Wladfa; Williams questions the idealized image of the colony that its own histories spread.

fuentes/como-fue-la-inmigracion-irlandes.texto: How Irish Immigration to Argentina Was
Juan Carlos Korol and Hilda Sabato

A study of Irish immigration to the province of Buenos Aires in the nineteenth century, tied to the expansion of sheep farming: the Irish arrived as laborers and shepherds, and many became sharecroppers and landowners. It analyzes their regional origin (the counties of Westmeath, Longford, and Wexford), their community life, and the role of Catholic chaplains.
It is the reference work of Argentine historiography on the Irish; it shows that their arrival came before the great wave of immigration and depended on networks of kinship and neighborhood.

fuentes/gaelic-sources-of-macpherson/res.texto: Thomson, a Gaelic poet and scholar, compares Macpherson's poems with the Gaelic ballads of the Fionn cycle preserved in manuscripts and in the oral tradition of the Highlands, and identifies those he used in each passage. He concludes that Macpherson knew that tradition well, but rewrote it freely, changed the characters and setting, and added most of the text.

fuentes/gaelic-sources-of-macpherson/por.texto: It closed the discussion of Ossian with an intermediate answer between total forgery and translation, and showed that behind the invention there was authentic Gaelic material.

fuentes/iolo-morganwg-y-los-poemas-agreg.texto: Iolo Morganwg and the Appendix Poems

Williams demonstrates that the poems added as an appendix to the 1789 edition of the work of Dafydd ap Gwilym, the greatest medieval Welsh poet, were written by Iolo Morganwg, and explains his methods: imitation of the ancient language, false attributions, and invented manuscripts.

It was the beginning of the critical study of Iolo's papers, which Williams continued throughout his life. Since then his work has been read as literature and as the history of ideas of the eighteenth century, not as a source on the druids or on the Middle Ages.

fuentes/the-invention-of-tradition/resum.texto: A collection of studies on traditions that present themselves as ancient but arose in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Hugh Trevor-Roper argues that the short Scottish kilt and the tartans of each clan were creations after 1707, with Ossian as a piece of the invention of the Highlands, and Prys Morgan studies the romantic search for the Welsh past: the Gorsedd, the Eisteddfod, Iolo Morganwg, and the Welsh national costume.

fuentes/the-invention-of-tradition/por_q.texto: It gave a name to a concept widely used in the study of nationalisms and of the Celtic. Trevor-Roper's chapter was criticized for exaggerating how invented the tartans were and for its disdainful tone toward the Highland Scots.

fuentes/the-festival-of-lughnasa/titulo.texto: The Festival of Lughnasa: A Study of the Survival of the Celtic Festival of the Beginning of Harvest

fuentes/the-festival-of-lughnasa/resumen.texto: A folklore study based on the archives of the Irish Folklore Commission, which gathers about two hundred places in Ireland where, at the end of July or the beginning of August, people climbed a hill, visited a holy well, or held a fair, such as the Puck Fair in Killorglin or the pilgrimage to Croagh Patrick. MacNeill interprets them as survivals of the medieval festival of Lugnasad and of a myth about Lug.

fuentes/the-festival-of-lughnasa/por_que.texto: It is the largest collection of data on a traditional Irish festival and an essential reference on the subject. Its thesis of a continuity from pagan antiquity was disputed by those, such as Ronald Hutton, who point out that most of these customs are documented only in the last few centuries.

fuentes/fallo-regina-contra-price/soport.texto: Judge's direction to the jury at the Cardiff courts (February 1884), published in the Law Reports

fuentes/fallo-regina-contra-price/resume.texto: Judge Stephen examined whether burning a corpse was an offense in English law and concluded that it was not, provided it did not cause public nuisance, although preventing a judicial inquest into the death was an offense. William Price, who had burned the body of his son in a ritual he said was druidic, was acquitted.

fuentes/fallo-regina-contra-price/por_qu.texto: It was the precedent that allowed the first legal cremations in the United Kingdom (1885) and the Cremation Act of 1902. It shows how a nineteenth-century neo-druid ended up influencing the law by an unexpected route.

fuentes/censo-de-la-isla-de-man-de-2021/.texto: Government of the Isle of Man

In the 2021 census, 2,223 people, 2.6 % of the island's 84,069 inhabitants, said they could speak, read, or write Manx (or some of those things); of them, 2,023 said they spoke it. In 2011 there had been 1,823 (1,662 spoke it), and in 2001, 1,689.
It documents the slow growth of Manx speakers as a second language almost half a century after the death of the last native speaker.

fuentes/guia-del-derecho-irlandes-tempra.texto: A Guide to Early Irish Law
Book (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, Early Irish Law Series 3)

A systematic account of the law in Irish texts of the seventh and eighth centuries: social hierarchy, honor and its price, contracts, clientship, the family, women, land, offenses and their compensation, and the role of judges or brehons. Kelly shows that it is a law of compensation and not of penalties imposed by a state.

It is the standard introduction to early Irish law. It discusses the old thesis (by D. A. Binchy, among others) that this law preserved Indo-European institutions almost intact, and points to the influence of canon law and of the clerics who committed it to writing.

fuentes/discurso-de-mitterrand-en-bibrac.texto: Speech by François Mitterrand on Mount Beuvray

Mitterrand declares Bibracte a “national site, a prominent place in the history of France”, recalls that the Gauls there chose Vercingetorix to lead the war against Caesar, and announces state support for the excavations. He warns that Bibracte “is not all of our past” and that the Gauls are part of the ancestry of the French, alongside others.

It shows the use of the Gauls by a socialist president of the late twentieth century: as a symbol of national unity, but with a plural idea of the origin of France and an archaeological project of European scope.
Text of the speech on the website of the Presidency of France

fuentes/asterix-el-galo/soporte.texto: Comic serialized in Pilote (1959-1960) and as an album (1961), with drawings by Albert Uderzo

fuentes/asterix-el-galo/resumen.texto: The first adventure of Asterix: in 50 BC, when all of Gaul is occupied by the Romans, a village in Armorica resists thanks to the magic potion of the druid Getafix. A centurion orders the druid captured to learn the recipe, and Asterix frees him by cunning.

fuentes/asterix-el-galo/por_que_importa.texto: It launched the best-selling European comic series, which fixed for generations of readers a humorous image of the Gauls. Its humor depends on anachronisms and nineteenth-century clichés that archaeology does not support, and on the play with national stereotypes of postwar France.

fuentes/os-celtas-en-galicia/titulo.texto: The Celts in Galicia: Archaeology and Politics in the Creation of Galician Identity

fuentes/os-celtas-en-galicia/resumen.texto: A historiographical study of how the idea of a Celtic Galicia was built: from José Verea y Aguiar and Manuel Murguía in the nineteenth century, using the hillforts and megaliths as proof, to the Galician nationalism of the twentieth century and the postwar archaeology, and the relation of each version to the political projects of its time.

fuentes/os-celtas-en-galicia/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the critical reviews of Galician Celticism from the standpoint of archaeology; it shows that the identification of hillforts with Celts was more a political need than a conclusion from the data.

personas/george-buchanan/resumen.texto: Scottish humanist who wrote in Latin, was tutor to King James VI, and in De iure regni apud Scotos (1579) defended the people's right to depose a tyrant king. In his Rerum Scoticarum Historia (1582) he argued that the first inhabitants of Britain and Ireland had come from Gaul and Hispania and that their languages were related to Gaulish, an idea that Edward Lhuyd took up and expanded in 1707. Studies of the modern origin of the word “Celtic” applied to the islands (Simon James, 1999; John Collis, 2003) start from him, because no ancient author called the Britons or the Irish Celts.

personas/edward-lhuyd/resumen.texto: Welsh naturalist and antiquarian, assistant and from 1690 keeper of the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford. Between 1697 and 1701 he travelled through Wales, Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall, and Brittany copying manuscripts, inscriptions, and vocabularies, and in the first volume of his Archaeologia Britannica (1707) he compared Welsh, Cornish, Breton, Irish, and Scottish Gaelic and grouped them with Gaulish under the name of “Celtic” languages. The modern use of “Celt” for the peoples who speak those languages comes from that work.

personas/paul-yves-pezron/resumen.texto: Breton Cistercian monk, abbot of La Charmoye, devoted to biblical chronology. In Antiquité de la nation et de la langue des Celtes (1703) he presented the Celts as descendants of Gomer, grandson of Noah, made the titans of Greek mythology into Celtic kings, and argued that Breton and Welsh preserved the language of the ancient Gauls. Translated into English in 1706, the work spread in Wales and Brittany the idea of a common and glorious Celtic past.

personas/john-toland/resumen.texto: Irish philosopher, deist, and republican, who left unfinished a critical history of the druids, published after his death (1726). A twentieth-century neo-druidic tradition presented him as the founder in 1717 of a druidic order in London; Ronald Hutton showed that there are no documents from the period to prove it.

personas/william-stukeley/resumen.texto: English physician and antiquary who between 1719 and 1724 measured and drew Stonehenge and Avebury with a care that archaeology still uses. Ordained in the Church of England in 1729, he published Stonehenge (1740) and Abury (1743), where he attributed both monuments to the druids, whom he presented as priests of a patriarchal religion related to Christianity, and he called himself “Chyndonax”. Stuart Piggott, his biographer (1950), separated the value of his field records from the fantasy of his interpretations: Stonehenge is some two thousand years older than the first documented druids.

personas/james-macpherson/resumen.texto: Schoolmaster and poet of the Scottish Highlands who between 1760 and 1765 published, as translations of Ossian, a third-century Gaelic bard, prose poems in English that were successful throughout Europe. He never showed the ancient manuscripts he said he had used; the Highland Society commission (1805) concluded that he had drawn on real Gaelic ballads but had composed, joined, and changed a great deal, and Derick Thomson (1952) identified the ballads that served as his basis. He later became a member of Parliament in London and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

personas/samuel-johnson/resumen.texto: English writer and critic, author of the Dictionary of the English Language (1755). After travelling through the Hebrides with James Boswell in 1773, he wrote in A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775) that the Ossian poems had no originals and that Scottish Gaelic had never been a written language; the first point was confirmed by the 1805 commission, the second was false, since medieval Gaelic manuscripts existed. When Macpherson threatened him, he replied in a letter that he would not stop denouncing what he believed to be an imposture.

personas/iolo-morganwg/resumen.texto: Stonemason and poet from Glamorgan who copied and gathered Welsh manuscripts and at the same time wrote poems and treatises that he attributed to medieval bards, with a supposed druidic tradition preserved in his region. In 1792 he held in London the first Gorsedd of the bards, a ceremony he invented and which since 1819 has formed part of the Eisteddfod. He was a radical, an opponent of slavery, and a Unitarian. His inventions, published in the Myvyrian Archaiology (1801-1807), the Iolo Manuscripts (1848), and Barddas (1862), were taken as authentic until Griffith John Williams dismantled them in the 1920s, without denying the value of his copies of genuine texts.

personas/charlotte-guest/resumen.texto: English aristocrat, married to the owner of the Dowlais ironworks in Wales, which she ran after being widowed. Between 1838 and 1845 she published, with the Welsh text and her English translation, the tales of the Red Book of Hergest and other manuscripts, with the help of Welsh scholars such as Thomas Price and John Jones (Tegid), and she popularized the name Mabinogion for them.

personas/hersart-de-la-villemarque/resum.texto: Breton nobleman who published in 1839 the Barzaz Breiz, a collection of Breton folk songs with a French translation, which he presented as remnants of the poetry of the ancient bards. From the 1860s on, François-Marie Luzel and others accused him of having invented or retouched the texts; the field notebooks studied by Donatien Laurent (1989) showed that many songs were indeed collected from oral tradition, although La Villemarqué corrected them, completed them, and attributed to them an antiquity they did not have.

personas/amedee-thierry/resumen.texto: French historian, brother of Augustin Thierry. His Histoire des Gaulois (1828) was the first complete history of the Gauls and presented them as the people from whom most of the French descended, as opposed to the Franks, from whom the aristocracy claimed descent; he divided the Gauls into two “races”, the Gauls and the Cymry. He was a prefect and senator under the Second Empire.

personas/napoleon-iii/resumen.texto: Nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte, president of the French Republic (1848-1852) and emperor (1852-1870). He wrote a Histoire de Jules César (1865-1866), created the Commission for the Topography of Gaul (1858), had Alesia excavated (1861-1865), founded the Museum of National Antiquities at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, and erected a statue of Vercingetorix at Alesia. His interest in Caesar and the Gauls drove French archaeology and at the same time served to legitimize his regime. He lost the throne after the defeat at Sedan (1870) and died in exile in England.

personas/matthew-arnold/resumen.texto: English poet and critic, professor of poetry at Oxford between 1857 and 1867. In the lectures On the Study of Celtic Literature (1867) he attributed to the Celtic “race” feeling, melancholy, and imagination, judged it little suited to politics, and called for a chair of Celtic at Oxford, which was created in 1877. His stereotypes, partly taken from Renan, were later criticized as a colonial view that fixed the Celts in the role of the emotional, against English practicality (Malcolm Chapman, 1992).

personas/james-cowles-prichard/resumen.texto: English physician and ethnologist who in The Eastern Origin of the Celtic Nations (1831) showed, through comparisons of vocabulary and grammar, that the Celtic languages belong to the Indo-European family.

personas/adolphe-pictet/resumen.texto: Geneva linguist and artillery officer who in De l'affinité des langues celtiques avec le sanscrit (1837) showed the kinship of the Celtic languages with Sanskrit, at the same time as Franz Bopp. Later he tried to reconstruct the life of the ancient Indo-Europeans from their common vocabulary in Les origines indo-européennes (1859-1863).

personas/johann-kaspar-zeuss/resumen.texto: Bavarian philologist and historian, considered the founder of Celtic philology. His Grammatica Celtica (1853), written in Latin from the Old Irish and Old Welsh glosses in manuscripts from Würzburg, Milan, Sankt Gallen, and other libraries, showed by the comparative method that the Celtic languages are Indo-European and established their historical grammar.

personas/henri-d-arbois-de-jubainville/r.texto: French archivist and historian, the first professor of Celtic language and literature at the Collège de France (1882). He directed the Revue celtique and wrote on the earliest inhabitants of Europe, on Irish literature and early Irish law, which he compared with Homer and with the institutions of the Gauls.

personas/rudolf-thurneysen/resumen.texto: Swiss linguist, professor at Freiburg im Breisgau and in Bonn. His Handbuch des Altirischen (1909; in English, A Grammar of Old Irish, 1946) remains the standard grammar of Old Irish, and Die irische Helden- und Königsage (1921) studied the manuscript tradition of Irish heroic epic; he also edited texts of early Irish law.

personas/kuno-meyer/resumen.texto: German philologist who taught in Liverpool and from 1911 in Berlin. He founded the School of Irish Learning in Dublin in 1903 and its journal Ériu, edited and translated many early Irish texts, and was made an honorary freeman of Dublin and Cork, honors that were withdrawn in 1915 because of his German propaganda in the United States during the First World War.

personas/camille-jullian/resumen.texto: French historian, professor at Bordeaux and from 1905 at the Collège de France, in the chair of national history and antiquities. His Vercingétorix (1901) and his Histoire de la Gaule (eight volumes, 1908-1926) made the Gauls the origin of the French nation and the Roman conquest an interruption of their own development. He was elected to the Académie française in 1924; his patriotic reading, shaped by the defeat of 1870, was revised by later historiography.

personas/henri-hubert/resumen.texto: French archaeologist and historian of religions, curator of the Museum of National Antiquities and collaborator of Émile Durkheim and Marcel Mauss, with whom he wrote on sacrifice and magic. His synthesis Les Celtes, published after his death (1932), described the Celts as a civilization recognizable in language, archaeology, and institutions, without the racial explanations common in his time.

personas/kenneth-jackson/resumen.texto: English Celticist, professor at Harvard and from 1950 at Edinburgh. Language and History in Early Britain (1953) fixed the chronology of the changes that led from British to Welsh, Cornish, and Breton and traced the retreat of British before English. In The Oldest Irish Tradition (1964) he argued that the Ulster cycle preserved a “window” onto Iron Age society, a thesis rejected by J. P. Mallory and Kim McCone.

personas/stuart-piggott/resumen.texto: English archaeologist, professor of archaeology at Edinburgh between 1946 and 1977, who excavated at Stonehenge and the West Kennet long barrow. He wrote the biography of William Stukeley (1950), Ancient Europe (1965), and The Druids (1968), where he separated what the ancient sources say about the druids from what antiquaries and Romantics added to them.

personas/venceslas-kruta/resumen.texto: French archaeologist born in Saumur, who studied in Brno and worked at the Institute of Archaeology in Prague until 1971, when he returned to France. He was director of studies in European protohistory at the École pratique des hautes études (1972-2008), directed the CNRS Centre for Celtic Studies and the journal Études celtiques, and specialized in La Tène art. He wrote the script for the exhibition I Celti (Venice, 1991) and Les Celtes. Histoire et dictionnaire (2000); he died on 19 July 2026 in Le Chesnay-Rocquencourt. His critics, including John Collis, fault him for presenting the Celts as a unified European civilization, the “first Europe” of the title of that exhibition.

personas/christian-goudineau/resumen.texto: French archaeologist, specialist in Roman Gaul and professor of national antiquities at the Collège de France. In César et la Gaule (1990) and Le dossier Vercingétorix (2001) he read Caesar's Commentaries as a text written for his political career, and separated Vercingetorix from the sources of the national hero manufactured in the nineteenth century.

personas/kim-mccone/resumen.texto: Linguist and Celticist, professor of Old Irish at Maynooth University. In Pagan Past and Christian Present in Early Irish Literature (1990) he argued that medieval Irish literature is the work of Christian clerics who reworked the pagan past for their own purposes, against the “nativist” reading that saw in it a nearly intact pre-Christian oral tradition.

personas/john-collis/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, professor at the University of Sheffield, specialist in the European Iron Age and in oppida, who excavated at Aulnat, near Clermont-Ferrand. In The Celts: Origins, Myths and Inventions (2003) he traced the use of the word “Celt” from the Greeks to today, argued that applying it to Britain and Ireland is a modern invention, and criticized the model of a Celtic expansion from central Europe.

personas/simon-james/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, professor at the University of Leicester and specialist in the Roman army. In The Atlantic Celts: Ancient People or Modern Invention? (1999) he argued that no people of Britain or Ireland called themselves Celts before the eighteenth century, and that the Celtic identity of the islands was born with Lhuyd, Pezron, and modern nationalisms, without denying the kinship of the languages.

personas/raimund-karl/resumen.texto: Austrian archaeologist, professor at Bangor University in Wales, specialist in the Iron Age and in the society of medieval Ireland and Wales. Against the Celtic skeptics he defended a definition of “Celtic” that combines language, archaeology, and written sources without requiring a common ethnic identity, and he accused skepticism of ignoring linguistic and literary evidence.

personas/bryan-sykes/resumen.texto: British geneticist, professor at Oxford, who studied mitochondrial DNA and in 2000 founded the company Oxford Ancestors, which sold ancestry analyses. In Blood of the Isles (2006) he argued that most British and Irish people descend from settlers who came before the Celts and the Anglo-Saxons, and that the lineages he called “Celtic” came from the Iberian Peninsula; other geneticists criticized his samples of living people and the sale of genetic identities.

personas/stephen-oppenheimer/resumen.texto: British pediatrician and popularizer of population genetics. In The Origins of the British (2006) he argued, from the DNA of living people, that most of the islands' ancestry came from settlers who arrived from southern Europe after the last glaciation and that later migrations contributed little. Subsequent studies of ancient DNA (Olalde et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2022) instead showed large population replacements in the Chalcolithic and the Bronze Age.

personas/william-morgan-traductor/resume.texto: Welsh clergyman, later bishop of Llandaff and St Asaph, who translated the complete Bible into Welsh (1588). His translation gave Welsh a literary standard and a weekly presence in the churches, and it is counted among the reasons the language survived better than Cornish or Manx.

personas/daines-barrington/resumen.texto: English jurist and antiquary who in 1768 toured Cornwall looking for speakers of Cornish and found Dolly Pentreath in Mousehole. He told of it in a letter read to the Society of Antiquaries and published in Archaeologia (1775), and later made known the letter in Cornish from the fisherman William Bodinar (1776).

personas/dolly-pentreath/resumen.texto: Fishmonger from Mousehole, in Cornwall, baptized in 1692. Daines Barrington visited her in 1768 and described her as the last person who spoke Cornish, which made her famous; she died in December 1777. There were later speakers and partial speakers, such as the fisherman William Bodinar, who wrote a letter in Cornish in 1776, so her title of “last speaker” is a simplification.

personas/henry-jenner/resumen.texto: Librarian of the British Museum, born in Cornwall, who published A Handbook of the Cornish Language (1904), the starting point of the Cornish revival, with a language based on that of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. He was the first great bard of the Cornish Gorsedh (1928).

personas/ned-maddrell/resumen.texto: Isle of Man fisherman who learned Manx as a boy from a great-aunt in Cregneash, in the south of the island. In 1948 the Irish Folklore Commission recorded his speech and that of other elderly speakers, recordings that later served the revival of the language. When he died, on 27 December 1974, he was the last native speaker of Manx.

personas/alexander-carmichael/resumen.texto: Scottish tax collector who for half a century gathered prayers, blessings, and charms in Gaelic in the Hebrides and the Highlands and published them with English translation as Carmina Gadelica (1900). Later studies, based on his notebooks, showed that he corrected, completed, and embellished many texts.

personas/aime-millet/resumen.texto: French sculptor, author of the statue of Vercingetorix that Napoleon III had erected in 1865 on Mont Auxois, at Alise-Sainte-Reine, the site identified with Alesia.

personas/thomas-thornycroft/resumen.texto: English sculptor who worked from 1856 until shortly before his death, sometimes with his son Hamo, on a group of Boudica and her daughters on a war chariot. The bronze was cast and placed only in 1902, beside Westminster Bridge in London.

personas/william-price-llantrisant/resum.texto: Welsh physician from Llantrisant, Chartist and neo-druid, who wore clothes he believed to be druidic. In 1884 he burned the body of his young son, whom he had named Iesu Grist (Jesus Christ in Welsh); the judge who acquitted him stated that cremation was not illegal if it caused no nuisance, a ruling that paved the way for the Cremation Act of 1902.

personas/manuel-murguia/resumen.texto: Galician historian and journalist, husband of Rosalía de Castro and first president of the Real Academia Gallega (1906). In his Historia de Galicia (1865-1913) he made the Celts the origin of the Galician nation and, on the basis of that root, set it apart from the rest of Spain; this construction became the basis of political Galician nationalism. Later archaeology and historiography criticized the weakness of his evidence and the racial sense of his account.

personas/eduardo-pondal/resumen.texto: Galician poet from Ponteceso, trained as a physician, who brought Murguía's Celticism into poetry: his verses evoke bards, chieftains, and an oppressed Celtic Galicia. He published Queixumes dos pinos (1886) and wrote the poem “Os pinos”, whose first stanzas, set to music by Pascual Veiga, were performed as the Galician anthem in Havana in 1907.

personas/douglas-hyde/resumen.texto: Irish Protestant, son of a Roscommon clergyman, who learned Irish as a boy from the peasants of his area and collected their poetry and tales. In the lecture “The Necessity for De-Anglicising Ireland” (1892) he called for the recovery of the Irish language and customs, and in 1893 he founded the Gaelic League with Eoin MacNeill and others, which he presided over until 1915. He was the first President of Ireland (1938-1945).

personas/w-b-yeats/resumen.texto: Irish poet and playwright who in The Celtic Twilight (1893) gathered fairy tales and beliefs of the peasants of Sligo and Galway and gave a name to an aesthetic of the “Celtic twilight”. With Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn he founded the Irish Literary Theatre (1899), from which the Abbey Theatre emerged (1904). He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 and was a senator of the Irish Free State.

personas/lady-gregory/resumen.texto: Isabella Augusta Gregory, Anglo-Irish landowner of Coole Park, in Galway, who learned Irish and collected the folklore of her area. In Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) and Gods and Fighting Men (1904) she retold the Irish sagas in English with the syntax of the Kiltartan speech. She was a co-founder and director of the Abbey Theatre.

personas/rene-goscinny/resumen.texto: French comics writer who spent his childhood and adolescence in Buenos Aires, where he was educated at the Lycée Français. With Albert Uderzo he created Asterix in the magazine Pilote (1959), which he later edited, and he also wrote Lucky Luke and Le Petit Nicolas.

personas/albert-uderzo/resumen.texto: French illustrator, son of Italian immigrants, who created Asterix with René Goscinny (1959) and continued the series as illustrator and writer from Goscinny's death (1977) until 2009.

personas/alan-stivell/resumen.texto: Breton musician who popularized the Celtic harp, rebuilt by his father, and mixed traditional Breton music with folk and rock. His album Renaissance de la harpe celtique (1971) and his concert at the Olympia in Paris (1972) popularized the label “Celtic music”.

personas/michael-d-jones/resumen.texto: Welsh Congregationalist minister, principal of the theological college at Bala, who from the 1850s promoted a Welsh colony outside the British Empire where the language and religion of its settlers could be preserved. He put much of his fortune into the enterprise that took the settlers of the Mimosa to Patagonia in 1865, and he visited the colony in 1882.
