personas/abraham-matthews/resumen.texto: Welsh minister who arrived in Patagonia on the Mimosa (1865) and was one of the religious leaders of the Chubut colony. He wrote Hanes y Wladfa Gymreig (1894), the first history of the colony.

personas/lewis-jones-patagonia/resumen.texto: Welsh printer who in 1862 travelled with Love Jones-Parry to Patagonia to choose the site of the colony and negotiate with the Argentine government, and who in 1865 received the settlers of the Mimosa. He was leader of the colony and promoted the Chubut railway, whose terminus gave rise to Trelew, named after him (Tre-Lew, “Lewis's town”); he founded the Welsh-language newspaper Y Drafod (1891).

hechos/toponimia-celta/titulo.texto: The Celtic Place Names of Europe

hechos/toponimia-celta/resumen.texto: Greek and Roman authors, inscriptions, and Ptolemy's Geography record hundreds of Celtic place names formed with elements such as dunon, “fortress, hill” (Lugdunum, today Lyon; Verodunum, Verdun; Camulodunum, Colchester), briga, “height, stronghold” (Segobriga, Conimbriga, Brigantium), magos, “plain, market” (Rotomagus, Rouen), and nemeton, “sanctuary”. Many survive in present-day names. Their distribution helps trace the ancient area of the Celtic languages: briga predominates in the Iberian Peninsula and dunon in Gaul and Britain; in Hispania it is debated whether some are Celtic or from another Indo-European language.

hechos/nombre-de-paris/titulo.texto: Lutetia of the Parisii: The Name of Paris

hechos/nombre-de-paris/resumen.texto: Caesar mentions Lutetia in 53 BC, the oppidum of the Parisii on an island in the Seine, where he gathered an assembly of Gaul (BG VI.3), and in 52 BC the battle fought near it (BG VII.57-62). In the fourth century the city began to be called by the name of its people, as happened with other Gallic capitals (the Remi gave Reims, the Turones gave Tours), and Ammianus Marcellinus already calls it Parisii. The meaning of both names is disputed.

hechos/nombre-de-lyon/resumen.texto: The Roman colony founded in 43 BC by Lucius Munatius Plancus at the confluence of the Rhône and the Saône received a Gaulish name, Lugdunum, from which Lyon comes. The most accepted interpretation is “fortress of Lugus”, a Celtic god; another is “bright hill”. The Greek treatise On Rivers, attributed to Plutarch, tells that the founders saw ravens and that lougos meant raven in their language, an explanation that linguists do not accept. The same name lies behind the origin of Laon.

hechos/nombre-de-bohemia/titulo.texto: Boihaemum: Bohemia, the Land of the Boii

hechos/nombre-de-bohemia/resumen.texto: Tacitus (Germania 28) writes that the name Boihaemum preserved the memory of the Boii, a Gaulish people who had lived there before the Germanic Marcomanni, although the population had changed. The name combines that of the people with the Germanic haim, “home”, and gave rise to Bohemia and the German Böhmen. It is one of the few cases in which an ancient author explains the Celtic origin of a place name.

hechos/nombre-de-galicia/resumen.texto: The name of Galicia comes from that of the Callaeci, a people of the northwest of the peninsula defeated by Decimus Junius Brutus around 137 BC, which earned him the surname Callaicus; the Romans later extended the name to the whole region, Gallaecia. Whether the name of the Callaeci was Celtic is debated, and its resemblance to Latin Galli, “Gauls”, may be a coincidence. The Galicia of Poland and Ukraine has no connection with the Celts: its name comes from the city of Halych.

hechos/nombres-de-belgica-y-helvecia/tit.texto: Belgium and Helvetia: Ancient Names for Modern States

hechos/nombres-de-belgica-y-helvecia/res.texto: Caesar opens the Commentaries by dividing Gaul among the Belgae, the Aquitani, and the Celts, and writes that the Belgae were “the bravest” (BG I.1). Humanists called the Low Countries Belgica, and the state that separated from them in 1830 took the name Belgium. Switzerland keeps the name of the Helvetii in its Latin name, Confoederatio Helvetica, from which come the abbreviation CH and the figure of Helvetia on its coins. In both cases these are learned names recovered in the modern period, not a continuity of the ancient peoples.

hechos/nombre-de-londres/titulo.texto: Londinium: A Name of Disputed Origin

hechos/nombre-de-londres/resumen.texto: Tacitus mentions Londinium in his account of the revolt of Boudica, in 60 or 61, as a place much frequented by merchants (Annals XIV.33); archaeology dates its foundation a few years earlier, around 47-50. The Celtic etymology that was repeated for centuries, based on a personal name or on a root meaning “wild”, was abandoned by linguists; Richard Coates (1998) proposed a form earlier than the Celtic languages related to the Thames, and the question remains open.

hechos/palabras-celtas-en-el-castellano/.texto: Spanish inherited from Latin several words that Latin had taken from Gaulish or from the Celts of Hispania: the academic dictionary gives that origin to camino, camisa, carro, cerveza, legua, sayo, berro, brío, alondra, vasallo, embajada, cambiar, pieza, tonel, landa, losa, tranca, serna, and bresca, and with doubt to colmena; lanza would come from Celtiberian, and galgo from Latin gallicus, “dog of Gaul”. Pliny the Elder already says that alauda, “lark”, was a Gaulish word (Natural History XI.121) and names the cervesia drunk in Gaul (XXII.164). Other words that are sometimes taken as Celtic are not so for the dictionary: álamo comes from Gothic, and gancho and garza are of uncertain origin. Several of these etymologies, proposed by Joan Corominas, remain under discussion.

hechos/palabras-galas-en-el-frances/resu.texto: Gaulish left a few hundred words in French, many of them from the countryside, nature, and work: chêne (“oak”), bouleau (“birch”), if (“yew”), lande (“heath”), alouette (“lark”), mouton (“sheep”), charrue (“plough”), ruche (“beehive”), boue (“mud”), glaner (“to glean”), tonneau (“barrel”), and chemin (“road”). Many more survive in dialects and place names. Pierre-Yves Lambert (1994) points out that most of them passed through the spoken Latin of Gaul, and that Gaulish influence on French grammar or pronunciation is much more disputed.

hechos/palabras-celtas-en-el-ingles/titu.texto: Celtic Words in English and the British Hypothesis

hechos/palabras-celtas-en-el-ingles/resu.texto: Old English took very few words from the Brittonic spoken by the island's population (brock, “badger”; crag, “cliff”; tor, “hill”; coomb, “valley”), which Kenneth Jackson (1953) explained by the low prestige of that language among the newcomers. Later loans came from Gaelic and Irish, such as clan, glen, slogan, whisky, galore, and bog. Since the 2000s some linguists have proposed that Brittonic influenced English grammar (for example, in the use of do in questions and in progressive forms); most consider this evidence insufficient.

hechos/sistema-vigesimal-del-frances/tit.texto: French Counting by Twenties: A Disputed Hypothesis

hechos/sistema-vigesimal-del-frances/res.texto: Standard French says quatre-vingts, “four twenties”, for 80 and soixante-dix for 70, and Old French also used six-vingts (120) or quinze-vingts (300), which gave its name to a Paris hospital founded by Louis IX. The most widespread explanation is a Gaulish substrate, because Irish, Welsh, and Breton count by twenties. An influence from Norman or Scandinavian and a Vasconic substrate (Theo Vennemann, whose hypothesis most reject) have also been proposed. Against a Gaulish origin it is pointed out that ancient Celtic, like the rest of the Indo-European languages, counted by tens, that the vigesimal system of the insular Celtic languages became general only in the Middle Ages, and that Old French and the French of Belgium and Switzerland used septante and nonante.

hechos/arte-insular/resumen.texto: Between the seventh and ninth centuries, in the monasteries of Ireland and Britain, a style formed that combines the spirals and trumpet patterns of Iron Age La Tène art with the interlacing animals of the Germanic peoples and the Mediterranean models of Christianity. Its main works are illuminated gospel books (Durrow, Lindisfarne, Kells), metalwork (the Tara Brooch, the Ardagh Chalice), and stone crosses. It is the main visible continuity between the art of the ancient Celts and the Middle Ages; art historians prefer to call it “insular” rather than “Celtic”, because it brings together Irish, Pictish, and Anglo-Saxon traditions.

hechos/hallazgo-del-broche-de-tara/titul.texto: The Discovery of the Tara Brooch and the Celtic Revival

hechos/hallazgo-del-broche-de-tara/resum.texto: In 1850 a gilded silver brooch from the late seventh or early eighth century appeared near Bettystown, on the coast of Meath. The Dublin jeweller George Waterhouse bought it and named it “of Tara” to link it with the kings of Ireland, although it has no connection with that site. Waterhouse sold replicas, and the brooch became a model for the Celtic revival in the decorative arts, which in the following decades filled Ireland and Scotland with crosses, jewelry, and typefaces with interlacing.

hechos/abolicion-del-derecho-brehon/resu.texto: Traditional Irish law, preserved in texts of the seventh and eighth centuries such as the Senchas Már and applied by judges called brehons, remained in force outside the English zone throughout the Middle Ages, despite the prohibitions of the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366). After the Tudor conquest, English courts declared invalid succession by tanistry (the Case of Tanistry, 1608) and the division of land among kinsmen, and the attorney general John Davies justified its abolition in 1612. Together with the Welsh laws attributed to Hywel Dda, preserved in thirteenth-century manuscripts, it is one of the two Celtic legal traditions that came down to us written in their own language.

hechos/fiestas-celtas-en-el-calendario-a.texto: Celtic Festivals in the Present-Day Calendar

Medieval Irish texts, such as Cormac's Glossary (around 900), name four festivals at the beginning of the seasons: Samain (1 November), Imbolc (1 February), Beltaine (1 May), and Lugnasad (1 August). They survived transformed in the Christian and popular calendar: the eve of All Saints, St Brigid's Day, the May festivals, and the August harvest gatherings, of which Máire MacNeill (1962) documented some two hundred in Ireland. Ronald Hutton (1996) warns that many customs attributed to them, such as the costumes and pumpkins of Halloween, are documented only from the early modern period and cannot simply be traced back to antiquity. In 2023 Ireland made St Brigid's Day a national holiday, presented both as a Christian feast and as the heritage of Imbolc.

hechos/extincion-del-galo/titulo.texto: The End of the Gaulish Language

hechos/extincion-del-galo/resumen.texto: There is no single date: the Gauls gradually replaced their language with Latin between the 1st and 6th centuries. The last testimonies are indirect: the jurist Ulpian (3rd century) admits written trusts in the Gaulish language; Jerome (around 387) compares the language of the Galatians with that of the Treveri; Sulpicius Severus, around 400, has a character speak “in Celtic or, if you prefer, in Gaulish”; Sidonius Apollinaris (around 474) praises Ecdicius for having made the Arvernian nobility abandon “the crust of Celtic speech”; and Gregory of Tours, in the sixth century, recalls a temple that in the Gaulish language was called Vasso Galatae. Alderik Blom (2009) and others warn that some of these texts may refer to the spoken Latin of Gaul and not to Gaulish.

hechos/retirada-del-britano/titulo.texto: The Retreat of Brittonic before English

hechos/retirada-del-britano/resumen.texto: At the end of Roman rule, around 410, Brittonic, the ancestor of Welsh, Cornish, and Breton, was spoken across almost the whole island south of the Picts. Between the fifth and eighth centuries it retreated before the Old English of the Anglo-Saxons: Kenneth Jackson (1953) traced, from the surviving Brittonic river names, successive zones of advance from east to west. Cumbric, the Brittonic of Strathclyde and Cumbria, died out around the eleventh or twelfth century. How much of this was due to migration and how much to the local population switching languages is debated; genetics (Leslie et al., 2015; Gretzinger et al., 2022) indicates a significant migratory contribution that varied by region.

hechos/clausula-de-la-lengua/titulo.texto: The Acts of Union in Wales and the Language Clause

hechos/clausula-de-la-lengua/resumen.texto: The laws of Henry VIII incorporated Wales into the kingdom of England and provided that justice and administration would operate only in English, and that no one who used Welsh could hold office unless he also used English. The Welsh nobility became anglicized, while most of the population went on speaking Welsh until the nineteenth century.

hechos/traduccion-de-la-biblia-al-gales/.texto: William Morgan Translates the Bible into Welsh

Under an Act of 1563 ordering that the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer be translated into Welsh, William Morgan published the complete Bible in that language in 1588. The translation gave Welsh a literary standard and a presence in worship every week; Cornish, which never had a printed Bible, and Manx, which got one only in 1775, did not receive that support.

hechos/firma-de-los-estatutos-de-iona/re.texto: In 1609 Bishop Andrew Knox gathered the clan chiefs of the Hebrides on Iona and had them accept, in the name of James VI, statutes that obliged them to support the Protestant church, limit their armed retinues, expel the bards, and educate their heirs in English. A Privy Council act of 1616 ordered that English be established everywhere and that Gaelic, which it called a cause of barbarism, be abolished. It was the beginning of a sustained policy against the Gaelic language and culture.

hechos/desalojos-de-las-tierras-altas/re.texto: After the Jacobite defeat of 1746 and the abolition of the judicial powers of the clan chiefs, the landowners of the Highlands and the Hebrides evicted much of their tenantry to raise sheep, sometimes by force, as in Sutherland between 1807 and 1821. Tens of thousands of Gaelic speakers emigrated to the cities of the Lowlands, to Canada, and to Australia. Historians (Eric Richards, Tom Devine) debate the scale of the violence and the responsibility of the landowners, but all agree on its effect on the language.

hechos/muerte-de-dolly-pentreath/titulo.texto: The Death of Dolly Pentreath, the “Last Speaker” of Cornish

hechos/muerte-de-dolly-pentreath/resumen.texto: Dolly Pentreath died in Mousehole in December 1777. Daines Barrington, who visited her in 1768, presented her in 1775 as the last person who spoke Cornish, although in 1776 the fisherman William Bodinar wrote a letter in that language, and there were partial speakers and families that kept words, numbers, and prayers until the nineteenth century. Cornish had been retreating since the Middle Ages before English and the Protestant Reformation, whose English-language Book of Common Prayer provoked the rebellion of 1549 and accelerated its decline.

hechos/informe-de-los-libros-azules/resu.texto: In 1847 three English commissioners published an official report on education in Wales that attributed the ignorance and immorality of the people to the Welsh language and to Dissenting Protestantism. The reaction was so strong that the report was remembered as the “treachery of the Blue Books”. In some schools, before and after the report, the Welsh Not was used, a board hung around the neck of the pupil who spoke Welsh, although it was not official policy.

hechos/gran-hambruna-irlandesa/titulo.texto: The Great Irish Famine and the Irish Language

hechos/gran-hambruna-irlandesa/resumen.texto: The loss of the potato crop to blight between 1845 and 1852, and the insufficient response of the British government, caused around a million deaths and the emigration of more than a million people; the population of Ireland fell by more than 20 %. The worst affected were the poor of the west and south, where the Irish speakers were concentrated. The 1851 census counted 23 % of speakers, and in the following decades emigration and English-medium schooling turned Irish into a language of the rural west.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-liga-gaelica/resu.texto: On 31 July 1893 Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill, and others founded the Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge) in Dublin to keep Irish as a spoken language and to spread its teaching. In twenty years it opened hundreds of branches and classes and secured the teaching of Irish in schools and its compulsory status for entry to the National University. Although Hyde wanted to keep it out of politics, many leaders of the independence movement came out of its ranks, and Hyde left it in 1915, when the League declared for independence.

hechos/irlandes-primera-lengua-oficial/t.texto: Irish, the First Official Language of the Irish State

hechos/irlandes-primera-lengua-oficial/r.texto: The Irish Free State (1922) made the teaching of Irish compulsory in schools and required knowledge of it for public employment; in 1926 a commission delimited the Gaeltacht, the areas where it was still spoken. The Constitution of 1937 declared it the national language and first official language. A century later, 40 % of the population says they know Irish, but fewer than 72,000 speak it every day outside school, and in the Gaeltacht it continues to decline.

hechos/renacimiento-del-cornico/resumen.texto: Henry Jenner published in 1904 a manual for relearning Cornish; Robert Morton Nance proposed in 1929 a unified Cornish, based on the medieval texts, and in the 1980s and 1990s rival variants emerged. In 2008 a Standard Written Form was agreed, and in 2010 UNESCO stopped classifying Cornish as extinct and moved it to “critically endangered”. Today a few hundred people speak it, most as a second language, and some families pass it on to their children.

hechos/muerte-de-ned-maddrell/titulo.texto: The Death of Ned Maddrell, the Last Native Speaker of Manx

hechos/muerte-de-ned-maddrell/resumen.texto: Ned Maddrell died on 27 December 1974 on the Isle of Man; he was the last speaker who had learned Manx as a boy in a community where it was spoken. In 1948, at the suggestion of Éamon de Valera, the Irish Folklore Commission had recorded the last elderly native speakers, and those recordings, together with the Manx Bible (1775), later served the revival of the language.

hechos/renacimiento-del-manes/resumen.texto: The Society for the Manx Language (Yn Çheshaght Ghailckagh) was founded in 1899, when the language was already declining rapidly. After the death of Ned Maddrell (1974), a generation that had learned it as a second language took it into radio, signs, and schools: the Bunscoill Ghaelgagh, a primary school in Manx, opened in 2001. In the island's 2011 census, 1,823 people said they could speak, read, or write Manx, and in the 2021 census 2,223 did, of whom 2,023 said they spoke it; there are children who learn it at home.

hechos/retroceso-del-breton/resumen.texto: During the Revolution, Barère's report (1794) identified Breton with federalism and superstition, and the compulsory schooling of the Third Republic (1881-1882) imposed French; in many schools a pupil caught speaking Breton was punished with an object called “the sign”. Around 1950 more than a million people still spoke Breton, according to estimates by Fañch Broudic, but it stopped being passed from parents to children within one or two generations. A 2024 survey by the TMO institute for the Brittany Region estimated some 107,000 people who say they speak it very well or fairly well, half the 214,000 in the 2018 survey, with the average age falling from 70 to about 58. The French Constitution, which since 1992 has declared French the language of the Republic, prevented ratification of the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages.

hechos/fundacion-de-diwan/resumen.texto: In 1977 the first Diwan (“seed”) school, a non-profit association offering free education, opened in Lampaul-Ploudalmézeau, teaching in Breton through immersion. The network came to have dozens of schools, colleges, and a lycée; the French state refused to integrate it into public education because immersion did not conform to the Constitution, according to the Council of State (2002).

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sociedad-de-la-le.texto: The Welsh Language Society and Welsh-Language Television

After Saunders Lewis's radio lecture “Tynged yr Iaith” (“The Fate of the Language”, February 1962), young nationalists founded the Welsh Language Society, which ran campaigns of civil disobedience (painting road signs in English only, refusing to pay licences) and secured the Welsh Language Act of 1967. In 1980 the nationalist leader Gwynfor Evans threatened a hunger strike if the government did not keep its promise of a Welsh-language television channel, and S4C went on air in 1982.

hechos/lenguas-celtas-en-los-censos-reci.texto: The Celtic Languages in the 2021 and 2022 Censuses

In the 2021 census, 538,300 residents of Wales aged over three (17.8 %) said they could speak Welsh; in the 2022 Scottish census, 130,161 reported some knowledge of Gaelic (speaking, reading, writing, or understanding it) and 69,701 said they could speak it; in the 2022 Irish census, 1,873,997 said they could speak Irish, but only 71,968 spoke it every day outside the education system. For Breton there is no census: a 2024 survey estimated some 107,000 people who speak it very well or fairly well. In the Isle of Man census of 2021, 2,223 people said they could speak, read, or write Manx (2,023 spoke it), and in the England and Wales census of 2021, 563 gave Cornish as their main language, a question that does not count those who know it as a second language. The figures are not comparable with one another because each census asks different questions: most measure what people say they know, not how much they use the language.

hechos/lhuyd-agrupa-las-lenguas-celticas.texto: Lhuyd Calls the Languages of the Islands “Celtic”

Edward Lhuyd published in Oxford in 1707 the first volume of his Archaeologia Britannica, where he compared Welsh, Cornish, Breton, Irish, and Scottish Gaelic, showed their kinship with Gaulish, and called them “Celtic” languages. No ancient author had called the Britons or the Irish Celts, and they did not call themselves that. For Simon James (1999) and John Collis (2003) this is the moment when the Celtic identity of the islands was born; their critics (Megaw, Koch) reply that Lhuyd discovered a real kinship, even though the name was new.

hechos/stukeley-atribuye-stonehenge-a-lo.texto: Stukeley Attributes Stonehenge to the Druids

In Stonehenge (1740) and Abury (1743), William Stukeley presented the two monuments as temples of the druids, whom he described as priests of a patriarchal religion close to Christianity. The idea spread through books, engravings, and the neo-druidic groups, who have celebrated the summer solstice there since the early twentieth century. Archaeology dates Stonehenge to between 3000 and 1500 BC, some two thousand years before the first documented druids.

hechos/publicacion-de-ossian/titulo.texto: Macpherson Publishes the Poems of Ossian

hechos/publicacion-de-ossian/resumen.texto: Between 1760 and 1765 James Macpherson published Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Fingal, Temora, and The Works of Ossian, presented as translations of a third-century Gaelic bard. The poems were translated into almost all European languages and founded the Romantic image of a heroic and melancholy Celtic past; Goethe included them in Werther, and Napoleon was among their admirers. They were free recreations of medieval Gaelic ballads of the Fionn cycle, which Macpherson moved to Scotland and to antiquity.

hechos/polemica-de-johnson-y-macpherson/.texto: Samuel Johnson Accuses Macpherson of Imposture

In A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775) Samuel Johnson wrote that the Ossian poems had no originals and challenged Macpherson to show the manuscripts. Macpherson threatened him, and Johnson replied in a letter that he would not be intimidated by the threat of a ruffian. The controversy divided English and Scots: for many Scots, denying Ossian meant denying Scotland's past. Johnson was right about the originals, but he was wrong to say that Gaelic had never been written.

hechos/veredicto-sobre-ossian/titulo.texto: The Highland Society's Report on Ossian

hechos/veredicto-sobre-ossian/resumen.texto: After Macpherson's death, a commission of the Highland Society of Scotland, chaired by the writer Henry Mackenzie, gathered testimony in the Highlands and reviewed his papers. Its report of 1805 concluded that there were traditional Gaelic poems about Fingal and Ossian, but none like those published, and that Macpherson had completed, joined, and changed a great deal. In 1807 a supposed Gaelic original was published, which specialists consider a Gaelic translation of the English text.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-antigua-orden-de-.texto: Foundation of the Ancient Order of Druids

In 1781 a group headed by the carpenter Henry Hurle founded the Ancient Order of Druids in a London tavern, a fraternal and mutual-aid society with rituals inspired by Freemasonry and by Stukeley's image of the druids. It is the oldest of the neo-druidic orders that exist; none of them has continuity with the ancient druids, of whom no written or oral tradition survived.

hechos/primera-gorsedd/titulo.texto: Iolo Morganwg Holds the First Gorsedd on Primrose Hill

hechos/primera-gorsedd/resumen.texto: On 21 June 1792, at the summer solstice, Iolo Morganwg gathered a group of Welsh poets on Primrose Hill, in London, inside a circle of small stones, and held the first Gorsedd of the bards of the island of Britain, with rites that he said were inherited from the druids through the bards of Glamorgan. The ceremony was his own invention.

hechos/gorsedd-en-el-eisteddfod/resumen.texto: In 1819 Iolo Morganwg held a Gorsedd ceremony in the garden of the Ivy Bush in Carmarthen during an eisteddfod, a competition of Welsh poetry and music of medieval origin. Since then the Gorsedd, with its robes, its stone circle, and its archdruid, has presided over the ceremonies of the National Eisteddfod of Wales, held every year since the late nineteenth century and the largest festival in the Welsh language. It is a case of an invented tradition that became authentic for those who practice it.

hechos/desenmascaramiento-de-iolo-morgan.texto: Griffith John Williams Exposes the Forgeries of Iolo Morganwg

Iolo Morganwg left thousands of manuscript pages in which he mixed copies of authentic texts with poems, triads and histories of his own invention. John Morris-Jones had already denounced some of them from the late 19th century, and Griffith John Williams, who devoted his life to those papers, showed from 1926 which were forgeries and how they had been made. Until then, Iolo's “bardic tradition” had been cited as a source on the druids in history and religion books.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-academia-celtica/.texto: Founding of the Celtic Academy in Paris

In 1804, during the Consulate, a group of scholars, among them Jacques Cambry, Jacques-Antoine Dulaure, Jacques Le Brigant and Éloi Johanneau, founded the Celtic Academy in Paris (30 March) to study the antiquities, languages and customs of the Gauls, to whom they attributed dolmens and menhirs. It was the center of French Celtomania, which saw Breton as the language of the Gauls and of the first men; in 1814 it became the Society of Antiquaries of France, which abandoned those theses.

hechos/polemica-del-barzaz-breiz/titulo.texto: The Controversy over the Barzaz Breiz

hechos/polemica-del-barzaz-breiz/resumen.texto: In 1872 François-Marie Luzel, who also collected Breton folk songs, argued that many texts in La Villemarqué's Barzaz Breiz (1839) were not found in oral tradition and had been invented or rewritten. The controversy divided Breton scholars for a century; Francis Gourvil (1960) accused it of forgery. Donatien Laurent's thesis (1989), based on La Villemarqué's field notebooks, showed that many of the songs had indeed been collected, but that the editor reworked them and gave them an antiquity they did not have.

hechos/juicio-de-william-price/titulo.texto: The Trial of William Price and the Legality of Cremation

hechos/juicio-de-william-price/resumen.texto: In January 1884 the doctor and neo-druid William Price burned, in the open air near Llantrisant, the body of his five-month-old son, whom he had named Iesu Grist (Jesus Christ). Arrested and tried in Cardiff, Judge James Stephen ruled that cremation was not illegal if it caused no nuisance to third parties. The ruling allowed the first cremations in the United Kingdom and led to the Cremation Act 1902.

hechos/excavaciones-de-alesia/titulo.texto: Napoleon III Orders Excavations at Alesia

hechos/excavaciones-de-alesia/resumen.texto: For his History of Julius Caesar, Napoleon III commissioned excavations on Mont Auxois, next to Alise-Sainte-Reine, directed by Commandant Eugène Stoffel. The work uncovered ditches, remains of the siege lines described by Caesar, and weapons, and it fixed the location of Alesia there. The finds went to the National Museum of Antiquities, which the emperor had founded at Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

hechos/estatua-de-vercingetorix-en-alesi.texto: The Statue of Vercingetorix at Alesia

In August 1865 a copper statue of Vercingetorix, almost seven meters tall and the work of Aimé Millet, was unveiled on Mont Auxois. According to many contemporaries, its face resembled that of Napoleon III. The pedestal bears a phrase inspired by Caesar: “Gaul united, forming a single nation, animated by one spirit, can defy the universe.” For Michael Dietler (1994) and Christian Goudineau (2001), the statue is an example of how the Second Empire used the Gauls to present itself as the heir of national unity.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-ubicacion-de-ales.texto: The Debate over the Location of Alesia

In 1855 the architect Alphonse Delacroix proposed that Alesia was at Alaise, in the Franche-Comté, and not at Alise-Sainte-Reine, in Burgundy; Napoleon III closed the discussion with his excavations. In 1962 André Berthier proposed Chaux-des-Crotenay, in the Jura, a hypothesis that still has defenders. The Franco-German excavations directed by Michel Reddé and Siegmar von Schnurbein between 1991 and 1997 confirmed the siege works at Alise-Sainte-Reine, the location that nearly all archaeology accepts.

hechos/estatua-de-ambiorix/titulo.texto: The Statue of Ambiorix in Tongeren

hechos/estatua-de-ambiorix/resumen.texto: In 1866 a statue of Ambiorix, chief of the Eburones, who destroyed a Roman legion and a half in 54 BC, was unveiled in the main square of Tongeren, the oldest city in Belgium. The work of the sculptor Jules Bertin. The young Belgian state, born in 1830, looked to him, and to Caesar's remark that the Belgae were the “bravest,” for a national hero predating the division between Flemish and Walloons. Ambiorix remained a popular figure in comics and schoolbooks.

hechos/nuestros-antepasados-los-galos/ti.texto: “Our Ancestors the Gauls” in French Schools

hechos/nuestros-antepasados-los-galos/re.texto: The school textbooks of the Third Republic, such as those of Ernest Lavisse, presented the Gauls as the ancestors of the French and Vercingetorix as the first national hero, in line with Amédée Thierry and Henri Martin. The formula “our ancestors the Gauls” was also taught in the colonies, where it became a symbol of the absurdity of assimilation. Michael Dietler (1994) shows that this genealogy served an idea of the nation united against Germany after 1870, and current historiography considers it a myth, because the population of France has very varied origins.

hechos/estatua-de-boudica-en-westminster.texto: The Statue of Boudica in Westminster

In 1902 a bronze group of Boudica and her daughters on a war chariot, modeled by Thomas Thornycroft between 1856 and 1885, was placed beside Westminster Bridge, opposite Parliament. The pedestal bears verses by William Cowper that prophesy for her descendants an empire greater than Caesar's. The queen who rebelled against Rome, according to Tacitus and Cassius Dio, became an emblem of the British Empire, and soon after a symbol of the suffragettes.

hechos/fundacion-del-abbey-theatre/titul.texto: The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre

hechos/fundacion-del-abbey-theatre/resum.texto: On 27 December 1904 the Abbey Theatre opened in Dublin, heir to the Irish Literary Theatre that W. B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn had founded in 1899. Together with the Gaelic League, it was the center of a literary revival that drew its themes from the Irish sagas, folklore and the life of the rural west, and that wrote mostly in English. Its nationalist critics reproached it precisely for that, and works such as John Millington Synge's The Playboy of the Western World (1907) caused riots over their image of the peasants.

hechos/estreno-del-himno-gallego/titulo.texto: The Premiere of the Galician Anthem in Havana

hechos/estreno-del-himno-gallego/resumen.texto: On 20 December 1907 “Os pinos” was premiered at the Centro Gallego in Havana, with lyrics by Eduardo Pondal and music by Pascual Veiga; it became the anthem of Galicia. The lyrics call Galicia “nation of Breogán” and urge it to awaken, in line with Murguía's Celticism. Breogán is a legendary figure of the Lebor Gabála Érenn, a medieval Irish history written by clerics, in which he founds Brigantia (probably A Coruña) and his descendants sail from there to Ireland; Galician Celticism made him the father of Galicia. It has been official since the 1981 Statute of Autonomy and the 1984 law on symbols.

hechos/celtismo-gallego/resumen.texto: From the mid-19th century, historians such as José Verea y Aguiar and Manuel Murguía made the Celts the origin of the Galician nation, and Pondal's poetry and the anthem spread the idea. Celticism was an argument for distinguishing Galicia from the rest of Spain and persisted in twentieth-century Galicianism, while Francoism used the Celts as the root of all Hispanic identity. Beatriz Díaz Santana (2002) and Gonzalo Ruiz Zapatero studied these political uses; current archaeology debates whether the castro culture of the northwest can be called Celtic and whether its language was, although place names and deities show Celtic elements. Galicia and Asturias take part in the interceltic festivals, but the Celtic League does not recognize them as Celtic nations because their languages are Romance.

hechos/vichy-en-gergovia/resumen.texto: On 30 August 1942, for the second anniversary of the French Legion of Combatants, the Vichy regime held a “festival of national unity” at the Vercingetorix monument on the Gergovia plateau, attended by Pétain and Laval: soil brought from every commune in France and the Empire was deposited in a crypt. The regime presented Vercingetorix, who had surrendered to save his people, as a forerunner of Pétain; the Resistance also invoked him. After the Liberation the Legion's inscription was removed.

hechos/mitterrand-en-bibracte/resumen.texto: On 17 September 1985 François Mitterrand visited Mont Beuvray and declared Bibracte, where according to Caesar the Gauls had chosen Vercingetorix as their leader, a “national site, a prominent place in the history of France.” In 1989 the European Archaeological Center of Mont Beuvray was created, and its museum opened in 1995. In the speech he warned that Bibracte “is not all of our past” and that “the Gauls are among our ancestors,” but that “we have many others”; Michael Dietler (1994) analyzed the project as a new, pro-European version of the political use of the Gauls.

hechos/exposicion-i-celti/resumen.texto: In 1991 the Palazzo Grassi in Venice, owned by Fiat, brought together Celtic objects lent by museums across Europe for the exhibition I Celti, with a committee of archaeologists led by Sabatino Moscati that included Venceslas Kruta, Otto-Herman Frey, Barry Raftery and Miklós Szabó. It was presented as the exhibition of “the first Europe,” in the year before the Maastricht Treaty. Michael Dietler (1994), Simon James (1999) and John Collis (2003) cited it as an example of the political use of the Celts in the service of European unity.

hechos/primera-aparicion-de-asterix/resu.texto: On 29 October 1959 the comic strip Asterix the Gaul, by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo, appeared in the first issue of the magazine Pilote. It follows a village in Armorica that resists Julius Caesar thanks to a magic potion brewed by the druid. With more than 390 million copies sold, it is the best-selling European comic series. Its humor plays with the clichés of the 19th century (the fighting Gauls, the bard, the druid, the boar feast) and with the national stereotypes of its time, and it fixed for the general public an image of the Gauls that archaeologists consider anachronistic: no winged helmets, no menhirs carried on their backs.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-liga-celta/resume.texto: In 1961 the Celtic League was founded at the Eisteddfod in Rhosllannerchrugog. It promotes the Celtic languages and the autonomy or independence of six “Celtic nations”: Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, those that kept a Celtic language or still spoke one in modern times. It continues the tradition of the Pan-Celtic congresses that began in the 19th century; the linguistic criterion leaves out Galicia and Asturias, which also claim their Celtic heritage.

hechos/festival-intercéltico-de-lorient/.texto: Polig Monjarret founded the Interceltic Festival in Lorient, Brittany, in 1971. Every August it brings together musicians, dancers and artists from Brittany, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, the Isle of Man, Galicia, Asturias and the Celtic diasporas. Together with the success of Alan Stivell and Irish groups such as The Chieftains, it consolidated “Celtic music” as a commercial category, which ethnomusicologists describe as a modern construction grouping distinct musical traditions.

hechos/nacimiento-de-la-filologia-celta/.texto: Johann Kaspar Zeuss's Grammatica Celtica (1853), which drew on the demonstrations by Prichard, Pictet and Bopp that the Celtic languages are Indo-European, turned their study into a scientific discipline. In the following decades the Revue celtique was founded (1870, Henri Gaidoz), along with the Celtic chair at Oxford (1877, John Rhys), the one at the Collège de France (1882, Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville) and the School of Irish Learning in Dublin (1903, Kuno Meyer). Germans such as Thurneysen and Meyer played a central role in the study of Old Irish.

hechos/debate-de-los-celtoescepticos/res.texto: From 1992 the anthropologist Malcolm Chapman and the archaeologists Simon James and John Collis argued that “Celt” is a category imposed from outside: the ancients did not call the peoples of the islands by that name, the Iron Age shows no common culture brought by invaders, and modern Celtic identity was born in the 18th century. Vincent and Ruth Megaw (1996), John Koch and Raimund Karl answered that the kinship of the languages, La Tène art and the texts are real, and the Megaws attributed the skepticism to English political motives, which James rejected. Barry Cunliffe continued to use the term in his synthesis The Ancient Celts (1997). By the mid-2000s the debate had calmed into a partial agreement: the idea of a homogeneous Celtic people arriving through invasions was abandoned, and many adopted Patrick Sims-Williams's proposal (1998) to use “Celtic” in a linguistic sense, while others (Karl, Fernández-Götz) kept studying collective identities in the Iron Age without assuming a single people.

hechos/genetica-popular-de-los-celtas/ti.texto: The Popular Genetics of the Celts

hechos/genetica-popular-de-los-celtas/re.texto: In 2006 Bryan Sykes (Blood of the Isles) and Stephen Oppenheimer (The Origins of the British) argued, from the DNA of living people, that most Britons and Irish descend from very ancient settlers, partly arriving from the Iberian Peninsula, and that later contributions were small; the press summed this up as Britons being “Celts” or “Basques.” Ancestry companies, Sykes's among them, sold “Celtic” or “Viking” origin certificates, which the geneticist Mark Thomas and the organization Sense about Science (2013) compared with astrology. Ancient DNA later disproved those continuities: there were almost total population replacements with the Bell Beaker (Olalde et al., 2018) and new migrations in the Bronze Age (Patterson et al., 2022).

hechos/estudio-de-leslie-2015/resumen.texto: In March 2015 the People of the British Isles project published in Nature its analysis of 2,039 people from the United Kingdom, from long-established rural families. It found that central and southern England form a fairly homogeneous group, while Wales, Scotland, Cornwall and Northern Ireland are divided into local groups very different from one another: there is no genetically common “Celtic” population. It also estimated that the Anglo-Saxons contributed less than half of the ancestry of central and southern England.

hechos/cristianismo-celta-moderno/resume.texto: Since the 1980s a “Celtic Christianity” has spread in Britain, Ireland and the United States, presented as closer to nature, egalitarian and more favorable to women than the Roman church, with prayer books, pilgrimages to Iona and Lindisfarne, and texts drawn from the Carmina Gadelica. Donald Meek (2000), Ian Bradley (1999) and Wendy Davies showed that there was no separate “Celtic Church” apart from Rome: the churches of Ireland and Britain had their own customs (the date of Easter, the tonsure) but recognized the pope, and the Synod of Whitby (664) discussed those differences, not a schism.

hechos/llegada-del-mimosa/titulo.texto: Arrival of the Mimosa and Founding of the Welsh Colony of Chubut

hechos/llegada-del-mimosa/resumen.texto: The sailing ship Mimosa left Liverpool on 28 May 1865 with 153 Welsh settlers and reached Golfo Nuevo on 28 July, a date Chubut celebrates as Welsh Landing Day. Organized by Michael D. Jones with the agreement of the Argentine government, which sought to populate Patagonia, the colony settled in the lower valley of the Chubut River, where Rawson was founded on 15 September, named after Interior Minister Guillermo Rawson. The first years were marked by hunger and drought; the settlers survived through exchange with the Tehuelche and with government aid, until they built irrigation canals.

hechos/ataque-del-valle-de-los-martires/.texto: The Attack in the Valley of the Martyrs

In March 1884, during the campaigns of the Conquest of the Desert, a group of Indigenous people attacked four Welsh settlers who were exploring the interior of Chubut toward the Andes: three were killed, and John Evans escaped because his horse, Malacara, jumped a ravine. Welsh accounts remember it as a tragedy in a relationship that until then had been peaceful with the Tehuelche; current historiography places it within the violence of the Argentine military advance, which pursued the same peoples with whom the colony traded.

hechos/expedicion-de-los-rifleros-del-ch.texto: Between October 1885 and early 1886, the governor of the Chubut Territory, Luis Jorge Fontana, toured the interior with some thirty armed Welsh settlers, the Chubut Riflemen, and reached the foot of the Andes, at a valley that the Welsh called Cwm Hyfryd (“lovely valley”) and Argentines called 16 de Octubre. Welsh settlers later established themselves there and founded Trevelin.

hechos/plebiscito-de-1902/titulo.texto: The 1902 Plebiscite of the Welsh Settlers

hechos/plebiscito-de-1902/resumen.texto: During the British arbitration on the boundary between Argentina and Chile, the Welsh settlers of the 16 de Octubre valley expressed, at the Corintos River school on 30 April 1902, their wish to remain under Argentine sovereignty. The award of King Edward VII, of November 1902, left the valley in Argentina; the vote is remembered in Trevelin as a founding act, although historians debate how much it weighed in the decision of the arbitration commission, which relied mainly on geographic and occupation criteria.

hechos/el-gales-en-el-chubut-hoy/resumen.texto: Welsh was the language of the colony until the early 20th century, when Argentine schooling, military service and the arrival of immigrants of other origins imposed Spanish. Since 1997 the Welsh Language Project, funded by the Welsh government and the British Council, has sent teachers from Wales; in 2024–2025 it had 1,106 students enrolled in schools and adult courses, compared with 623 in 2020. There is no census of speakers: the Chubut government estimated about 1,500, and E. Wyn James of Cardiff University up to 5,000 people able to speak it. Gaiman, Trelew and Trevelin keep chapels, tea houses and the Eisteddfod, the annual poetry and music competition held in Welsh and Spanish.

hechos/inmigracion-irlandesa-a-la-argent.texto: Between 1830 and 1930, and especially between 1850 and 1870, thousands of Irish arrived in Argentina, most of them from the counties of Westmeath, Longford and Wexford. They worked as shepherds and farmhands in the expansion of sheep farming in Buenos Aires Province, and often became sharecroppers and landowners. They formed a Catholic community with its chaplains, such as the Dominican Anthony Fahy, and its newspaper, The Southern Cross (1875). Their descendants are estimated, without a census to measure it, at between half a million and a million, and most also have other origins. They spoke mainly English: Irish did not have in Argentina the continuity that Welsh had in Chubut.

lugares/museo-de-arqueologia-nacional/re.texto: Museum created by Napoleon III in 1862 under the name Museum of Celtic and Gallo-Roman Antiquities, later renamed National Antiquities, in the château of Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris; it opened in 1867. It brought together the finds from the excavations at Alesia and other sites of the conquest of Gaul, and today holds one of the largest prehistoric and Celtic archaeology collections in Europe.

lugares/monumento-de-gergovia/resumen.texto: A 26-meter monument of Volvic stone, raised in 1900 on the Gergovia plateau, near Clermont-Ferrand, to commemorate Vercingetorix's victory over Caesar in 52 BC. In 1942 the Vichy regime enlarged it and deposited soil from every commune of France in a crypt; after the Liberation the Legion's inscription was removed.
